PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
SHEETS of music are often bought by the choir. MARRIAGE is a science in which there are no experts.

1‘ Or, BRIDGET 1 / told you to notice when the apples boiled over." "Sure, I did, mum. It was a quarter-past eleven." MANY a coquette would be mortified if she knew how many hearts she could not break. Too many good resolutions are stronger at their birth than at any subsequent period. THE indulgent father keeps his spendthrift Sint in cheque. WHEN is a doctor most annoyed! When ha is out of patients. WE are apt to distrust those people who flatter us, and dislike those who do not.

HIS LAST ROPE.—Mamma—" No, Willy, there is no such person as Santa Claus." Little Willy —"ls George Washington a myth, too, mamma " THEy say that matches are made in heaven." "Possibly; but it's different with marriages. They're made almost anywhere." WHEN a rich man realises that money has not brought him happiness, he promptly turns his attention to doubling his supply of it. Two of the most pathetic sights on earth are man trying to cry over a woman's troubles, and a woman trying to laugh at a man's jokes. THE chief aim of some women's lives seems to be to get things cleaned up one day before it is time to clean 'em up for the next. THE REMAINING MYSTERY.—" Do you under. stand golf?" " Yes ; everything, except why anybody plays it." MRS. PECK: "Before we were married you vowed you would die for me." Poor Henry Peck: "Well, this is a living death."
DEPLETING.—Father: "If you will agree to a year's engagment, you can marry my daughter." Suitor: "But I won't have money enough then."

HEARD IN THE NIGHT.—" George ? " Yes, dear." "Oh, what did you wake me up for? I only wished to know if you had come home." "I CAN tell you," said he, " how much water runs over Niagara Falls to a quart." "How much?" replied she. "Two pints." "I SEE, said the man with the paper, "that there is a king in Africa who has been drunk for fifteen years." "That," said the cheerful idiot, "is what might be called a soaking reign." " Excusx me if I seem to be a little imperti- nent, but I must venture a question." "What is It ? " "Are you a gentleman going golfing, or a iady going cycling ? " INSURANCE AGENT: "Before filling the claim, will you be kind enough to give me a certificate of your husband's death, madam ? " The New Widow: "With pleasure." .. . . .
In spite Of what he tells his girl Man can any passion smother, Unless, indeed, he loves himself— And then he cannot love another.
A FATTIER solved the baby question in a remark, on his own as follows: "We would not take £lO,OOO for this one, nor give five shillings for another."

A SAFE PREVENTIVII—A farmer saw a recipf advertised for keeping the cisterns from freezing in winter. Having sent stamps he had a reply: "Take in your cistern at niaht, and stand it in front of the fire." HEARD WHILE MAMMA WAS OUT.—" Does the baby look like you or your wife ? " "Well, it depends somewhat on how he feels; when he's good-natured he resembles me, but at other times I eau see a great deal of his mother in him. ,AT THE FOOT.—"I hope they don't give my little boy any naughty nicknames in school?" "Yes, ma; they call me 'Corns.'" "How dread- ful 1 And why do they call you that ? " "Cause in our class, you know, I'm always at the foot." GUEST: "Who is that pale, frail-looking man with spectacles who comes here every morning and drinks a bottle of apollinaris ? " Bar-tender: "Why, that's the man who writes those lively drinking songs that the students like so." PAPA: "Charley, please hand me the book on the table there." Charley (aged nine) : "There he is, paps." Papa; "No, my son; you should not say 'There he is.' but it' is." Charley: "Why, papa, it's a hymn-book, isn't it?" MIKE : How old are you, Pat?" Pat: " Thirty- sivin next mont'." Mike: " Yez must be older than that. When were yez born?" Pat: "In 1860." Mike: "I have yez now I Sure, yez told me the same date tin year ago 1" WILLING TO PARTICIPATE.—His lordship—" I am deeply interested in the new gold discoveries." Friend—" You don't think of going to the Klon- dike, do you ? " His Lordship—" Oh, no ! But I thought of advertising that I should be glad to communicate with any successful miner who might happen to have an unmarried daughter." A BAD SIGN.—Mrs. Newkid "My dear, I don't think it is quite safe to have that doctor treat the baby." Newkid : "Why not ?" Mrs. Newkid : "Well, I've sent for him three different times, and each time he came so promptly that I'm afraid he hasn't many patients." A LONG-FELT WANT.—Simpkins : "I've got a patentable idea that I expect to make a fortune out of." Timkins : "What is it ? " Simkins :"A scarfpin shield that will prevent a man from gett- ing tangled up in his best girl's hair."

QUITE A PREJUDICE.—Guest (at country inn) : "It does NOM rather strange, landlord, but it really appears to me that the eggs were fresher in London." Landlord: "But that is only a preju- dice, sir. It is from London we get them."

• MK. DAKOTA: "It actually gets so cold up in our country that the dames freeze to the back of the grate and have to be chopped off with an axe." Mr. Mexico: "That's nothing to our heat; why, we have to filed our hens on choppad ice to keep them from laying boiled eggs."

"As thc imm."rtal William once said," remarked Prince Henry, •‘ there's a divinity that shapes our ends, rough-hew them how we will." "Really, now, Heinrich," said the Kaiser, as he overheard the remark of the Prince, "that is quite clever, but when did I say it:" "Ws a real pleasure to me to give you any- thing," he said as he forced the bouquet into her hand. "Stay," she replied, handing back the flowers; "you are like all the rest of the men. All you cate for is pleasure. Take the flowers; I cannot consent to encourage such selfishness." THE VALUE OF CLASSICAL MUSIC.—" I suppose classical music is all right in its place," said Maud. "I'm sure it is," replied Mamie; "I don't care to listen to it myself, but sometimes you have to play it in order to gat a man to go home."

"WHAT " said the judge, "you expect me to send your husband to prison when you acknow- ledge that you threw five flatirons at him, and hti only threw one at you?" "Yes, that's all right, judge," said the irate woman; "but then the one he threw hit me."

CAPABLE.—" You ask for my daughter, sir," observed the retired banker. "And you say your present salary is small. Do you imagine that would keep her in the style to which she had been accustomed?" "I do not, sir," answered the young man, as his lower jaw hardened perceptibly. What is good enough for me, however, is good enough for her." "Young man," said the man of money, with deep emotion, as he grasped the speaker's hand, "take her. You are just the sort I have been looking for. I have never had enough nerve to try to convince her of that myself."

-THEY were two women discussing their husbands. One asked the other if her husband was ever cross. "He is never anythir g else," was the cool reply. "How do you manage him?" asked the first speaker. "I don't try to manage him. I just let him alone. "But how do you make up?" "We don't make up. You see, he is always as cross as two sticks at breakfast, and says a lot of sarcastic things about women attending to their households, and then he goes a,wey in a pet and slams the front door." "You 000 r thing ! And people say'you are so congenial and so well suited to each other. "So we are. When Harold comes home at night he hands me a little package and says he hopes it will please me, and I tell him he is too good, and that I wish all women had as good a husband as mine; and I give him a kiss and ask him to forgive me for being cross in the morning." The other woman looked dazed and was silent as long as she could stand it. Then she said out: "And vet you deliberately told me von did not manage him."
THE MOST NUTRITIOUS.

div.p: EP 'S'S
GRATEFUL-COM FORTING.
CO CO
AREAKFAST AND SUPPER.
LADIES' LETTER.
ME DEAR NEEErE,

Velvet now appears to rank first and foremost as one of the favourite fabrics. For cloaks and gowns it will be equally popular, anti the graceful draped effect so eminently suited to its heavy folds, and ably carried out by the style which has now come to be known almost universally as "Liberty style," will be much worn. Sleeves in this fabric are for the most part in pagoda form, being edged with some gold or other handsome embroidery, and revealing an inner sleeve of white, generally of some soft diaphanous material, which in most cases will have a little berthe or chemisette to car. respond. A large buckle, confining the folds on shoulder or hip, is a greatfeatere in the new modes, which to all appearance is merely caught together carelessly, but I may add that only those who have attempted the task can realise how difficult it is to obtain this effect.

The toque is certainly the favourite headgear at present, but it is now so large that it has much in common with the ordinary hat, while there are many shapes in soft felt with crumpled brims which come midway between the two. Many of the most stylish and useful toques are of white or biscuit cloth with folded brims caught up in front or at the side with a huge rosette of cloth and a quill, or with a large paste or steel buckle. For afternoon wear toques of panne or miroir velvet, with wings set straight across the front, are in vogue, and some of the smartest have their brims covered with lace applique or gold- thread embroidery. Another pretty type of toque has the brim of tucked or corded cloth, and the crown of spotted or checked glace silk gracefully draped, a couple of velvet chrysanthemums be- ing tucked under the brim. The Toreador shape in felt and straw seems to be coming in once more, and for country wear Tam o' Shanters in cloth to match the coat and skirt are considered correct.

For walking gowns, satin-faced cloths and friezes continue most popular, but the pale pastel shades seem to be giving way to full decided colours especially claret, plum deep crimson, and beetroot-red. Skirts are still long, and when of heavy makes of material are simply ornamented with rows of stitching, cordings or narrow strap- pings of glace silk, but if of fairly light-weight cloths they are often most elaborate both in cut and trimming. A smart dress, for example, of beetroot cloth is made with a Princesse polonaise opening with rounded fronts over a petticoat of beetroot glace finely tucked and stitched. The fronts of the polonaise are faced with a wide band of thick, bold patterned ecru guipure which forms revers on the bodice. The same lace is used for the pointed vest and also for the under-sleeves, which are put into rather wide, tight wristbands of glace, the cloth upper sleeves being bell-shaped but not very large.

I notice that many women are wearing their hair dressed low on. the neck under their hats. Such a style is almost entorced by the low, flat hats which at present prevail. It is impossible to place them well on the head if the hair is gathered up into a high coil on top. With the toques, no— with the hats, yes—l think the coil at the nape of the neck looks best. Some are using handsome combs behind to keep the toque up, whilst a little jewelled brooch, round or oblong, to keep tidy the short loose hairs behind, is worn by all. Jewelled side-combs are much used, for the hairdressing does not greatly alter ; the hair is very slightly puffed out all round, and combed up full and high from the forehead in front.

The bolero, of course, as winter approaches, cannot command such a universal following as it has had of late, but it is still well to the fore. The newest shape has a pleat down the centre of the back, a mode not to be contemplated by the stout and dumpy figure. The banded bolero set into a band at the waist is also fashionable, and it is smart-looking.

For present wear a black velvet coat would be very nice. You might have a costume of one ot the new friezes in a nice red-currant shade or a greenish-blue, made with a loose coat, so that you could wear it with different shirts and blouses. You could wear this with the coat to match for mild weather, and with the black velvet coat when it is colder. For indoor wear a cashmere dress would be nice in a warm shade of brown, trin.uned with apricot on the bodice, and with one or two different blouses this would probably be enough, as you will have some old gown for second best. A black velvet toque would look nice with the velvet coat, and you might have a felt hat, trimmed with tucked glace silk, for the frieze costume.
Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: HOUSE BY THE RIVER.
div.p: THE HOUSE BY THE RIVER.
BY MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSON, Author of "The Secret of the Pearls," "The Honge by the Lock," "Queen Sweetheart," "The Barnstormers," "Her Royal Highness," /to.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPIERS: Lancelot Wade, a well-connected ne'er-do-well, lives with his daughter Sybil in fourth-floor rooms in Blooms- I;ury. One day the father brings Sybil the extraor- dinary news that she—she who never went anywhere vr saw anybody in her life—is to go to a dinner- party at Lady Northinuir's house in Berkeley-square, where she meets a certain Jack Churchill, who is expected by Lady Carstairs, +iiother guest, to marry her datiOiter Gladys. The dinner, like the house is very grand. and Sybil is supremely uncomfortable. Next morning Lancelot Wade does not appear at breakfast; Sybil finds that his bed has not been slept in. Alarmel, she is about to go to the police-station, when a messenger-boy appears:with a letter from her father. The envelope is blood-smeared, and the mesenger hesitatingly admits that he thinks there has been an accident. Sybil is conducted by t e messenger-boy, by means of trams and trains, quite out of the city to a lonely house on the river bank. She is told to enter a ceitain room, and, expecting to see her father, she unhesitatingly enters. The room is empty! And Sybil, when she tries to get out again, finds herself a prisoner. • Meanwhile Churchill, on his way to the birtnday-feast o! Gladys, reads of Lancelot Wade's suicide, and carries the news to Lady Carstairs. At the close of e last chapter they are discussing Sybil Wade's future.
CHAPTER VIII TIIE KINDNESS OP LADY CARSTAIRS.

"Do you think that it is our duty to provide a home for Lancelot Wade's daughter?" Lady Carstairs asked, bluntly. "I don't presume to think," Jack returned. "I only wondered if there was—er—anything your friends might be allowed to do also. For instance, a—a cousin of mine is looking for a governess for her little daughter." (Jack Churchill was a scrupulously truthful young man in general, but, somewhat to his own surprise, he invented the cousin and her daughter on the spot.) "I thought as Miss Wade had been abroad so much and must know a lot of languages, you see, she might be just the one my cousin is wanting—that. is, of course, if you—unless. you " _

His liesitatiCM deprecated the chance that Ikixly Carstairs might be actuated with a passionate desire to adopt the forlorn young beauty into her own heart and household. As for the governess idea— which had been a sudden inspiration—it would be easy enough to "live up to it., so to speak. Surely there must be some nice woman with a growing daughter who would be glad to take the girl if salary and expenses were provided for secretly by him ? "The poor little thing would never guess," he said to himself. "And, if Lady Carstairs doesn't want to be bothered with her she must have a pleasant, safe home somewhere—and she shall I" "You are very good. It is like you," responded Lady Carstairs, sweetly, while Jack wondered why he had never before observed what very thin lips she had. "Bat, you see, I was only trying you, half in fun, to find out exactly how big your heart was for the various waifs and strays of this world in whom you can't feel any personal interest. As a matter of fact we have already taken steps to provide for the young creature's comfort, so that you mustn't trouble your charitable head any more about her. I'm sure you have already far too many calls of the sort."

"I assure you I hadn't thought of Miss Sybil Wade as an object of charity," almost indignantly protested Jack. "She was so very sweet and winning, so beautiful in an innocent, childlike way—a sort of model for' Elaine, the Lily Maid of Astolat, ' it seemed to me—that naturally we hoped her future might—" "Quite so," interpolated Lady Carstairs, blandly. "How nice of you to think the poor child pretty. Gladys and I, I am sorry to say, found her extremely gauche and uninteresting; though, to be sure, what else could have been expected after the awful way in which she had been brought up? However, that is a detail, isn't it? Her unattrac- tiveness has little enough to do with our duty, and that plainly is—as you would have remarked, if you hadn't been afraid of hurting my feelings—to see that she wants for nothing. I was saying so to Gladys this afternoon as soon as we heard how that wretched man had made an end of himself. Wagn't I, Gladys, darling?" "Yes, mamma," returned Gladys, with unusual meekness.

She was daintily trifling with an entree now, and smiling with restored tranquillity. Never, it seemed to her, had she so valued and appreciated the admirable qualities of that tactful woman, her mother. She readily guessed the motive in Lady Carstairs's statements, but she waited with eager- ness what was to come next. What were they (to be supposed) ready to do for that impertinent, ill- bred girl Sybil Wade? "We at once wrote to the child," Lady Carstairs went on, then paused for an instant at a quick, warning glance from Gladys. What had she said that was wrong? "I was afraid that you had not got her address," remarked Jack.

"Ah !" Lady Carstairs understood Gladys's look now. "We did not have it, to be sure, the other day; but as it happened I had a note from Sybil only this morning, asking—er—asking if we had heard anything about her father, who had mysteriously disappeared. No doubt Lancelot thought that she would be sure to apply to us sooner or later. Of course, the note prepared us, more or less' for the—er—terrible discovery that came later. And as soon as I had recovered from the shock I wrote at once, on Lady Northmuir's authority, asking her to come for the present to Berkeley-square. I sent the letter by hand, and just before Gladys and I came out this evening I received a reply. Let me see, did I by any chance slip it into the pocket of this gown ? " She felt in the vague, helpless way that women do feel for objects presumably placed in the elusively-situated pockets of their modern gowns, and Gladys watched her, with ever-growing admiration. Really, her mother was a remarkable woman! What presence of mind! What daring Gladys began to be almost as excited as if she were watching thescrucial act of a play. "Dear me, no! I must have left it on my desk," Lady Carstairs regretfully concluded. "If I had had it I should have liked, since you take so kind an interest, to read out one or two paragraphs in the letter to you. However, I can remember the purport of it—rather disillusionising, alas Sybil had heard of her father's death and expressed her- self, though naturally shocked, as being scarcely surprised. (It appears that he had often threatened something i of the kind.) Then she went on to thank me—it would be unkind to criticise the poor girl's spelling—for offering to take her in; but she preferred remaining where she was till after the funeral. She had made great friends with the landlady of the lodging-house where she and her father had stayed since coming to England, and the landlady's son and daughter. I fear they are very common persons, but, no doubt, more of the sort to Whom she has been accustomed all her life than we are. From one or two hints she gave I—really, I don't know if I ought to mention it, but we are talking very inti- mately now—l should not be surprised if there were something under the rather particular way in which the girl wrote about the extraordinary kind- ness of the landlady's son. Didn't you fancy so, Gladys ? " "I felt sure of it. Ugh What a prospect of a new family connection for us " exclaimed Gladys, shrugging her lovely white shoulders and shudder- ing prettily. "Sybil added that a gift of money would be acceptable," Lady Carstairs continued, "and, of purse, I at once despatched a cheque as I had intended all along to do. I shall go and see her some time to-morrow—before you call for our little talk about that unfortunate mistake of the orchids, perhaps—and then, if you haven't lost interest, you shall hear all the latest developments. As for the funeral, I believe Carstairs will attend to everything—not a very pleasant task for him, poor boy—and probably it will take place almost imme- diately. But I don't think that Gladys or I need know anything about that. Our duty will have been done in providing for Sybil until she marries, which we have quite made up our minds to' do." As she finished Lady Carstairs breathed a sigh —the resigned and peaceful sigh of the virtuous matron who feels that she has acquitted herself well in trying circumstances and at last earned the right to rest. Jack Churchill was almost literally struck dumb by the flood of information that she had imparted. Somehow—why, he could hardly have defined—he felt horribly unhappy. Plunged into the deepest

gloom. tie ought to have a mind relieved of its weight after hearing of the kindly interest Lady Carstairs manifested in the girl for whom he had cherished such yearning pity. Sybil Wade was not alone and dependent on strangers for aid. Her own relatives stood ready to "take her up" and do what was right by her, no matter how small was the meed of affection they gave. She had no need of anything that he could do, which fact should have gratified him. And what concern was it of his if she had fallen in love with the son of a woman who let lodgings? He could not forget the girl's exquisitely modulated accents, her dainty, girlish dignity and charming, shy naivete. All that Carstairs and Gladys had said was powerless to make him fancy Sybil Wade other than a "perfect little thoroughbred "—the words with which he mentally described her; so that he was certain no innate vulgarity of soul could have drawn her to a lover who was not a gentleman, at least, in heart. "It's nothing against a man that his mother lets lodgings," Jack assured himself, gloomily. "He may be one of Nature's noblemen, and a genius of the first water to boot, for all that we can tell; but —but—oh, well, somehow I feel as if somebody had been rubbing a file across my front teeth. By Jove What a fool I am! I suppose I wanted a chance to pose as knight-errant for a pretty girl; and, now that I know she doesn't want me and has plenty of others to do her service, I'm mean enough to be down in the dumps." At all events, there was nothing that he could offer to do without making himself actually officious, and in all probability, he thought, he should never see Sybil Wade again. A vague sense of loss lay heavily upon him. He was glad when the birthday-feast was at last over, and Lady Carstairs rose to go. A carriage had been sent by Lady Northmuir, and Jack breathed more freely when it had rolled away. For a moment he stood gazing absent-mindedly after it, his hat in his hand, the light shining down on his frank, clear-cut face and close-cropped, curly brown hair. "Queer at out those orchids, with their gold ribbons and diamonds," he said. "Who could have sent th(in to her pretending they had come from me—and why ? "
The smile with which Gladys Carstairs had bidden Jack Churchill "good-bye" died a sudden death when the necessity to be charming no longer existed.
"What a failure! What a hateful, hateful failure!" she exclaimed.

"Not at all, Gladys. Your judgments are always too hasty," said Lady Carstairs, rescuing the unfortunate orchids from annihilation on the floor of the brougham. "Wait till Mr. Churchill and I have had our little tete-a-tete conversation to- morrow before you say anything about failure." "He has not the slightest intention of proposing," Gladys returned, snappishly, "or he would have behaved very differently about the bouquet. I hated him when he said so quietly that he 'couldn't claim credit for such good taste.' It was just as if he meant to hint, at the same time, that neither had he the good taste to select me." "Nonsense " cried Lady Carstairs. "Jack Churchill isn't the sort of man to deal in hints and double meanings. Last week I was certain that, if he were not absolutely in love with you, he was hovering so near the edge that he only needed a skilful little push to be helped over and realise his own condition."

"So did I think so. And then we arranged that skilful little push with the orchids lest he shouldn't discover his feelings without our assistance. But, after all, it was worse than useless, only humiliat- ing me for nothing. What if he should find out or guess that the diamonds were paste, the ribbon tinsel, and the whole thing what Carstairs would call a put-up job '? " "It is impossible that he can find out. I have provided against that, at least, without the slightest danger of failure. And he would never suspect U 9 of planning such a coup. Men's brains are very different from women's—our sort of women—not so subtle, not so good at finesse. I was certainly justified in hoping that he was chivalrous enough and cared enough for you to take the responsibility of sending the present upon himself rather than you should be shamed by learning that you had been made the victim of a trick. But I suppose women can't always expect to know what men are likely to do in given circumstances. We only know what we want them to do, and think they ought to do—aggravating creatures! Once he had led you to believe .he had sent the orchids he could no longer have gone on with this dreary, tedious, monotonous game of friendship. The lovers'-knots in the ribbon, and the apparent significance of the gift, would have been almost equivalent to a declara- tion, which must certainly have followed, since we admit that he is an honourable man. And if nothing had been changed since last week I feel sure that matters would have gone on as I had planned without the slightest hitch." "You mean that there's been a change in his feelings towards me since last week, a change in three days?" commented Gladys, sulkily. "I don't care a rap for Jack Churchill, really, and if he wasn't one of the richest men in England I wouldn't have him if he wiled me a hundred times over. Still, it does make me furious to think that, when almost any other man I know would be ready to go on his knees if I so much as held out a finger, this nouveau riche, this upstart, turns away from me to look at a white-faced, insignificant little nobody like Sybil Wade. For I suppose you mean me to understand that you fear it is the meeting with her which has produced the sudden change ? " "I fancy it. I don't fear' it," corrected Lady Carstairs. "If there was ever any danger from that direction I rather think I have put an end to it." She laughed faintly and Gladys echoed her laugh. "You were wonderful! How did you ever think of it all? The story flowed along like—like an incoming tide." "I always thought I might have had a talent for fiction if I had needed to earn my own living. Now, when your brother Carstairs is making him- self so disagreeable about our few debts, and altogether shewing himself most ungrateful to me and unbrotherly to you, it struck me that for once I might make the old 'talent useful. I did rather flatter myself on the amount of realistic detail I filled in." _

"Well you might," rejoined Gladys, appre- ciatively. "But now, you see, we must live up to the story. Unexpected things always happen; and though it seems most unlikely that, in the natural course of events, Jack Churchill should ever run across Sybil Wade, still we must somehow make it sure that he doesn't."

"I had thought of that, of course," rejoined Lady Carstairs, defending her own diplomacy. "There was just this foundation for my tale. I will go and see the girl to-morrow morning early, before Mr. Churchill comes to make that call which I intend shall go far towards deciding his fate and yours. Naturally we told him, when he was tactless enough to suggest the other day that she should be asked to the Savoy f, r your birtheay- dinner, that Lancelot Wade had 14t no add, es 3. It was quite safe to say so, for I was cer an Mr. Churchill hadn't heard him mention ti e number of the house and street in Bloomsbury. But I remember perfectly well it was 28, Mitchell-street, and no doubt Sybil is there still. I will get Mrs. Iremonger—that woman you've heard me speak of, who is a superintendent, or sorra thing of the sort, for a curious kind of half-charit tble school for orphan girls—to take Sybil as n teacher. The woman is always writing begging-letters for dona- tions, and I will promise to send her twenty pounds and mention the charity to my fr'enis if, 9,3 a favour to me, she finds a place for this girl and promises to keep her on. The school is in Scotland, at the other end of nowhere; and, once there, we need not fear that word of Sybil Wade will ever come to Jack Churchill's ears again. Besides, we shall really have done the proper thing in providing for her welfare." "Where's the 'w rty pounds to come from ?' asked Gladys, glcomily. 'lf Carstairs remains in his present humour we are not to have a penny over the regular allowance ever again, and not even that till our debts are paid off. Oh, who could wonder that I am ready to do almost anything to secure the chance of marrying a man who, whatever his faults may be, has unlimited money, unlimited generosity ?" "I will tell Carstairs that ho must let us have this money, that your future settlement may depend on it. That will influence him, cross as he is at present (really, I never knew him so strange in his manner!), for he is certainly anxious to get you off his hands." "When can you see him?" complained Gladys. "He seems determined lately to keep as much as possible out of your way." "I must make an opportunity," said Lady Carstairs. As she spoke the brougham topped before the house i Berkeley-square, and tLe footman sprang down to throw open the door. At that moment, as if Pate had provided the opportunity of which she had just spoken, Lord Caretairs was coming down the two or three steps from the house to the street.

I have something most important to say to you." Thus adjuring IThr son she hurriedly stepped out "Carstairs 1" she exclaimed. -Carsta.irs, wait! of the broughani, all her draperies trailing over the pavement, in her determination to detain him al all costs. div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

It was a happy idea of Her Majesty to send a contin- gent of Imperial troops to Australia on the occasion ot the forthcoming visit of the Duke and Duchess of York, to open the first parliament of the new Commonwealth- The guard of honour will be furnished by the various branches of the British army, including the volunteers, and they will naturally increase the interest in the pro- ceedings in which their Royal Highnesses are to take part. The Duke and Duchess have arranged to leave in March, and their tour will extend over four or five months. What with the visit to Australia and the re- turn of the troops from the war, the coming year seems likely to make some heavy demands upon the time and services of various members of the Royal Family. . _ _

The reception accorded in London to-the C:ty imperial Volunteers, recalls the great jubilation over the return of the Brigade of Guards from the Crimea in 1856. The people were on tbat occasion, sn carried away with en- thusiastic manifestations of welcome, that the troops had the greatest difficulty in making their way from the station to Buckingham Palace, where the Queen accom- panied by her children, received the gallant Guardsmen. Later on Her Majesty in company wi:h Prince Alberc,re- viewed the Brigade in Hyde Park, and there was after- wards a grand firework display and illuminations. It is expected that the Queen will hold a great review of British troops, returned from the war, early in the spring. This will probably take place in Windsor Park, but the disbandment of the C.l.V.'s will presumably prevent them from taking anything but a spectacular part in these proceedings. The writers who have betrothed the young Chleen of Holland, to almost all the unmarried Princes in Europe, have no opportunity for furtherispeculation in that par- ticular respect. There remains however, the oppor- tunity for ingenious folks to tell us how the engagement came about, what the Queen thought on the subject, and so on. These details are being supplied, as might have been expected, and with of course, the stereotyped addi- tion that it is" purely a love match." When the wed- ding takes place we shall probably be supplied with other details of the betrothal, different in every partici).- lsr from the versions now given except the clauie in re- ference to" a love match."

Few people could probably explain the origin of the word " spinster " es applied to unmarried women. There is however, no dcubt that it comes to us from the custom of former times, that no woman should marry till with her own hands she had spun a complete set of personal, bed, and table linen. From this custom the law adopted the phrase "spinster," which to this day is the legal and official definition of au unmarried woman. Another custom not uncommon in former times, was that of being married with the church key. From time immemorial, even among the ancient people of the earth the gift of a wedding ring was considered a necessary part of the marriage ceremony, but it was not always terthcoming, and in olden times, not infrequently some device, such as the church key, had to be made use of , before the marriage was solemnised. Society is always seeking after a new diversion, and failing the discovery of new games it falls back upon old ones. Thus when lawn tennis began to flag, we tell back upon croquet, and now it seems that not only are we to have a revival of roller-3katiog this winter, but the ancient game of dominoes is once more to become fashionable. Instead of the many silly competitions. that have been tacked on to afternoon tea in recent years, we are to return to this game of our childhood, though of course, dominoes properly played is a real game of skill. There is also just as much fashion about musical In- struments. Everybody knows how aociety took up with the banjo some years ago. This was followed by the mandoliu, and this in turn must give way to the zither, which is to be tbe popular instrument this winter. To a large extent crancing still holds its own as one of the chief resources of the winter, but even this is less popu- lar than it was, and there is clearly an open held for anyone who can discover a new game or amusement of an attractive and sensible character,for both indoor and outdoor diversion.

The tcque, boa, and muff, must, if we would be in "fashion's van,' harmonise. Thus, they must be built entirely or shew a trimming of, the same fur, or velvet, or other fabric. Not all of us can aspire to a set of furs. at their present inflsted prices, but few amorg us possess not a few odd pieces which, with a little discre- tion and nimbleness of fingers, can be turned to such excellent use. To begin with, the brim only of the toque need be of fur, the crown being composed of cloth, velvet, or panne. to match the gown with which it is to be wern. Then if uur resources make a Laos Unattainable, perchance we can line the collar and revers of the coat with the pieces that lie to hand, or at least outline the same with the fur. Then the muff. This can bo built of the same fabric as that which cocapoees the crown of the toque,the front only being of the fur, or should our stock have run very low, bands of the same arranged slantwise, will blend the three articles into the necessary " harmonious whole." With regard to the boa fashionable, this should be flat not round (as was the mode last year) and lined with quilted satin, or better still, panne. The muff linins should match, and the colcur, to be correct,should repeat the relief tint employed for the costume. The collar of the moment in all up-to-date tailor made coats, is Napoleonic, in cut, not unlike the double linen collar, patronised by fashienable men for some time past This collar sometimes goes by the name of the Cossack, and the Austrian, but the shape is one and the same. Unquestionably it is a great improvement on the " storm "variety, which must have been worth consi- derable sums, to doctors and physicians. It is a very great mistake to coddle, and more especiall7 to coddle one's throat and neck. That the Irish should win the first award—£loo—at Earls Court, in connection with the " Women of all Nations," surprised none among us who had se.n and weighed their charms for ourselves. With her dark hair, glorious eyes, and brow, soft velvety skin and beautiful graceful form, the charm of our sister from the Emerald Isle was unapproachable. England stood second, Scotland third, and Canads last in the money prizes, and Japan first on the hat for medals. This wa in great measure due to the sweet little Japanese baby, whose quaint, droll ways, as ebe toddled anout—utterly unconscious of the crowds' scrutiny—amused and fascin- ated everybody. There are, in different peosles national characteristics about the hands as well as in the colour of the eyes and hair. As a ruleaJrish girls have the most beautiful hands In Britain women have usually too fleshy and plump bands. The hands of the Ameriean girls are long and narrow, while the fingers of the German women are too short, and the palms too bread. The hands of the French, Italian, and Spanish girls, are generally indif- ferent, Us. ugh the Parisians bestow a great deal of pains en their hands, and many people would be deposed to say that they have finer hands than the women of any other country.

Black eyes, like black hair, usually indicate good powers c-f physical gandurance. By those who claim to have studied the subject,it is stated that the dark haired races are physically the strongest. but less endowmd in- tellectually than the fair-haired. Grey eyes denote quick- ness of temper, and desire for novelty. Efsz-1 belong to shrewd natures, and such as delight in intercouss with friends. Clear blue eyes are associated with love of change an I progress. Blue and grey eyes are only found in tbe cold and temperate regions, which have produced the higb'y cultivated and prcgressive nations.

div.head: WARRINGTON SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON SOCIETY.
Lecture on "Longfellow."

The winter session of the Warrington Society was opened on 'Tuesday evening, when an excellent paper on " Lnngfellow " was delivered by Mr W 11 Woodcock. Mr W H J Jenkins, who presided, said the object of such meetings was to encourage and develop a love of literature. The Lecturer brififly traced the poet'e early life. As a young man, he said, he was accemplished ann even learned. At the age of 33 he had puolished " Outre Mer " and " Hyperion," and written widely in literature. Spe acing of the poet's work generally, be said be did not know a single poem he would wish he had never written. lie bad given them many bald, unpoetic and unsatisfactory lines, but throughout his work they saw strong and continual evidences of sound judgment and ripe scholarly taste unmarred by the slightest soupcon of anything to offend the most sensitive. His rare spirit of industry never allowed him to grow slatternly, and his last published poem breathed the same purpose and was couched in as happy and appropriate language as the rest of his work. They must not go to Loegfellow for philosophy or rhapsodies or jingling rhyme or heights and depths of passion and pathos. An ardent student of nature, he would never become a scientist or metaphysician. To read the moral turnings he repeatedly gave even to his simplest poem, and which he never appeared to overlook, seemed so natural, yet he believed the cold abstractions of meta- physics to have been beyond his power to deal with. Though deeply religious, the poet was no bigot or sectarian. Strongly conscious of sin and vrrew he was not pessimist enough to see only bad in the world, ner optimist sufficient to see only good. A craftsman of unerring taste, he never allowed himself to fall into a slavish adherence to conventiooal forms nor to paint eny:hing by the sham colours of artificiality, and whilst adeering to recognized forms and methods he was ever ()pin to the gloms of a new light, with the rereiltant spentaneity of verse which showed a perpetual primeval freshness; never lapsing into vagueness and eccentricity.—The Chairman said they had listened to a very charmine. pap,r. He was glad that Mr Woodcock had struck the true nito of the p -weer character. Long- fellow was esi•eltially a poet of the hc me,and dealt with the duties rine tires: of life. There was always some- t,-,ing in his poetry in the nature of a solace. The lecture WAS further di.cussed by Councillors Bennett and F R Roberts, Dr Naden, and Mr Fulton Smith, and a short reply by Mr Woodcock brought the meeting to a close.

Society asked him if he rul(J clone to the gathering that afternoon e answered " Yes I will come, because I a'elleve that religion is practical. If we are to make it or ese in the world we want to be practical." ighteousness, jußtice, and humanity. (Applause.) He hoped that the twentieth century would see one universal Cbriitian Empire— a spectacle of unity that angels would delight to behold—a type of that celestial unity. Where saints of all ages in harmony meet Their Saviour and brethren transported to greet.

e _ He ventured to say, with pain, that there was no stumbling-block t—ore effe-tual, and that impeded the onward march of Christianity more than the bitterness that disgraced the controversies of the Christian Church. (Applause.) The Church had been guilty of the heresy of exalting religious opinions and ritual into higher prominence than moral purity. What was needed to-day was the earnest application of the principles of Christianity to the condition of our everyday life. It was not enough to try now and again in special services to convert men by repeatiug dull,pious nlatitute and by raving and singing hymns so thin and threadbare that there was very little meaning left in them. He knew that the supreme business for which the Church of God existed was to save men from their sins ; but it was the supreme business of the Church also to save men not from a possible hell of the future but from the hell of the present and make this world what it ought to be—a paradise of God. (Applause.) Religion had no meaning no justification unless it spiritualized the life and interests and recreation of the masses of the people. He hoped that the time was not far distant when members of all Churches should stand in one solid phalanx, and putting aside that miserable spirit that dwarfed and degraded the grandeur of Clue._ tianity, work together to promote the best interests of the town, and thus save it from its evils and distressess' (Applause.) 'fhere was a great deal in the circumstance of the last ten months which was perplexieg and con" flicting. They honoured the brave men who had nobly endured and heroically died for Queen and country. They held high the memory of those who to night were sleeping on the veldt el South Africa. They felt to-day that the country was on the eve of great changes. Many disturbing problems were being force 1 upon the puhlic mind ,The world was everywhere conceiving new thoughts The unchanging East was passing through its revolu - tion ; and he was delighted to read last night the prin- ciples of the action accepted by Germany and Great Britain—principles which would tend to peace. He hoped that the issues ancii destinies ot the Chinese Empire would be wisely ordered by the great powers of the world (Applause.) However sanguine they might be as to their country's future, they could not wisely ignore that there were dangerous elements in our national life that threatened the demoralisation of some of our best institutions. Thoughtful students and observers of passing events could not fail to recognise that there were influences which might greatly cripple our ship of State. The dangers which confronted us as a nation to-day were not from without, but from within—dangers against which mighty armies and ships of war were powerless. If he was asked! to mention some single cause more potent than every other in the production of wretchedness and vice in these closing days of the century, he should say without hesitation, that it was the decay in family religion and disruption of family life. As a rule the profligacy that paraded our streets, and the drunken- ness that degraded our land, were evidences of a decline in domestic moral discipline and •eiety. The degradation of the poor by overcrowding in our towns and cities, and the enervation of the rich by their seclusion in suburbs and in luxurious villas— threatened the purity and vigour of an old fireside family life. In these days we were apt to overlook this qaestion. Empire was in the air. We talked and swaggered about nothing less than Empire. We spoke as if we had a monopoly of divine grace. We 1 boasted that we were members of an Empire in which the sun never set, and we were legitimately proud of that great colony which was soon to ripe into the dignity of a commonwealth beneath the 'Southern Cross. (Applause.) In these momentous das s when confronted by Imperial responsibilities greater and more urgent than have ever been felt in the long history of our race —when excitements caused by the war concealed even

from religious people the great urgency and importance of grave moral questions—in these days, whose din and dust and excitement had drowned and darkened the wisest and brightest thoughts of our greatest teachers, he ventured to remind them of a great principle which underlay all social and national greatness. The family was God's primary type of every community and beneath all the developments of the divine ideal— family, tribe, state, nation' Empire—was the family still. The nation that failed to comply with , the condition involved in this great principle was a nation that was doomed to fall. (Applause.) No nation could stand that disregarded the conditions of social and national prosperity. We hoped that our great ally America would succeed in its great task. (Applause ) There was no brighter omen for the dawning of the 20th century than the desire of these two great nations for a more cordial fellowship and co-operation in the great service of mankind. What God bath joined together let no man put asunder. (Applause.) Why did Germany defeat Frence ? The scenes of the Franco-Gem war were within the recollection of most of them. The French were defeated because the homes of Germany were purer than the homes of France. He did not wish to say anything at this hour derogatory to France,but woe to the nation that was not faithful enough to grapple with its own vice and infamy. We had been at peace with France for 65 years. God grant that this peace might not be broken. (Applause.) Zola,in current literature, attributed the de- cline of France to overmuch religion, a most ridiculous excuse, for religion was the secret of a nation's greatnesa. What would Zola say when the late High Priest of the Transvaal, Oom Paul, commenced ;his missionary tour in France ? (Laughter.) Righteousness was the only sure foundation upon which the fabric of national life could be safely built up. There were many causes which controlled the development of empires. Home lies at the foundation of England's social greatness. If our empire was to escape the fate which overtook the empires of the ancient world, we must see to it that the ' life of England was pure and clean at its source, we must see to it that the holy day of rest was not made a day of idle pleasure, and do all we could to put down the senseless betting and gambling which drove so many young fellows to vice and crime. (Applause.) We stood very near to the portal of the 20th century, and we could not think witheut solemn awe of the possibilities, opportunities, and obligations, which rest upon us as a people. Let them plead for a higher ideal of citizenship —of domestic life—and stand together in defence of the great principle of righteousness, justice, and humanity. (Applause.) A collection was taken and realized £7 13s. 85., mak- ing a total for the day of £l5 4s. 2d.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR AT WARRINGTON.

Child's Body Found on a Doorstep. A shocking discovery was made early on Monday morning, in Arpley-street. Mrs Ho'ford residing at 15, Arpley-street had occasion to open the yard gate, and saw a brown paper parcel on the step. Iler suspicion was aroused, and she sent for a police- officer. He opened the parcel and found the dead body of an infant. Later in the day a post-mortem examination of the body was made by the police- surgeon, Dr Smith, who found that the child had had a separate existence. An inquiry into the circumstances attending the death was conducted in the evening at the Police Station, by Mr Brighouse, county coroner. Jane Holford, wife of George Holford, shirt manufacturer, 15, Arpley-street, stated that at a quarter past seven in the morning she had occa- sion to open the yard door, and saw a brown paper parcel, in the shape of a box on the step. Her sus- picions became aroused and she sent for the police. Constable Hamblett came, and on opening the par- cel found the dead body of a child. P.C. B amblett said the body was that of a male child. be brought it to the Police Station, where Dr. Smith made a post4mortem examination. Dr. Smith, police surgeon, gave the result of the examination. The body was that of a fully devel- oped male child. It was decomposing. There were no marks of violence. The lungs were full of air. The stomach contained air, but no food, The brain was conges:ed. The Coroner; Do you think the child had a separ- ate existence? Witness: Yes. Continuing his evidence, the witness observed that the body was wrapped in a silk handkerchief with one corner cut off. The child was probably born towards the end of last week. It might have lived a few hours. Ho thought the cause of death was inatteeition at birth. He should say that the child was allowed to die. Inspector Phillips: You do not think there was medical attendance at birth? Witness: ICo not think there could have been, The Coroner said they could not carry the matter further. Upon the information given to the jury the police would make inquiries. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the child haO a separate existence and died from inattention at birth. Chief Inspector Phillips said the police would institute inquiries.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, OCTOBER 26, 1900. SALT TRADE RUMOURS AND REALITIES.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, OCTOBER 26, 1900. SALT TRADE RUMOURS AND REALITIES.
[From the LivEarooL JOURNILL or COMUEIICE, Oat. 21, 1900.]

The rumour of some inventioa in the salt trade which is likely to C4Llie a beneficial change in the process of manufacturing table salt or white salt, to which we re- ferred a montn ago, has been revived in a modified and interesting form. It is said that a powerful chemical manufacturing company is likely to take up the new process and work it, and rumour new goes so far as to assert that the company in question is effecting an ar- rangement with the principal salt manufacturing com- pany, of the nature of an amalgamation, for the work- ing of the new process and of the salt business of the old salt company. Whatever credence may be placed upon such a rumour in London, it is perfectly certain that those who are most directly in- terested in th.. salt trade in Liverpool and Cheshire view it as a fabrication for share-dealing purposes. There is, in the first place, still no knowledge analog members of the salt trade in Liverpool of any invention or new method of mauufacturi ag salt which is likely, in the near future, to take the place of the old method. As pointed out in our previous references to the matter, there is a strong presumption against any invention or change of process forthcoming which would be likely to prove of material service to the salt trade, owing to the well-known conditions of supply and demand. Italian and Spanish salt is now being offered at prices which would leave English salt manufacturers in the throes of a keen competition, even were they able to save 25 or 30 per cent, on their present cost of production. The source of the troubles in the English salt trade are seemingly inexhaustible supplies of cheap salt which have been opened up in America, on the Continent, in Arabia, Africa, and Australia. Instead of England being the principal source of supply for these countries, they are not only supplying themselves with salt, but are offering their abundant surplus to consumers in other countries. Using the heat of the sun as the evaporating agent, there is little or no plant required for the manu- facture, and consequently these large supplies of salt are available at an expense which enables producers in some countries to offer their salt at a much lower price than English producers can. This is the arms of the situation. As regards the suggestion that a large chemi-- cal manufacturing company is likely to come to an arrangement which will be equivalent to an amalgamation with the largest salt manufac- turing company, this suggestion, it may be said plainly, is more ridiculed than the previous one. The large chemical manufacturing company would have to be either the United Alkali Company or Brunner, Mond and Co., and the largest salt manufacturing company could only be the Salt Union. The United Alkali Com- pany happen to be salt manufacturers on a large scale. Up to the end of September they had this year exported 23,628 tons from their Fleetwood works, and in the near future this eempany are likely to be extensive brine pumpers at Wimboldeley, in Cheshire, where they recently acquired land in the salt district for the pur— pose of obtaining brine. There is no visible reason as regards the requirements of their own manufacture,or as regards the selling price of salt for export, why the United Alkali Company should desire to control the works of the Salt Union. It is highly•probable that even at Wimboldsley the United Alkali Company will carefully avoid the labour of manufacturing so profitless an article as salt, and will turn their brine to more direct and profitable account. as the other large chemical manufac- turers have done. The thought of Brunner, Mond and Co. taking over the works of the Salt Union may be dismissed as little short of ludicrous. Though in the Bowman, Thompson branch, which was lately arnalea- mated with Brunner,Mond,and Co., salt has been manu- factured, the basis of this great company's operations and profits is liquid brine, not dry salt. As regards their own manufacture, Brunner, Mond, and Co. have no scope for using the product of the Salt Union's works. They have a more scientific and profit- able method of dealing with sodium-chloride than evaporating it out as the salt mak ,re have done, and as an article for sale to the world outside of themselves salt is not nearly profitable enough to interest Brunner, Mond and Co. The rumour of amalgamation may, therefore, be;dismissed as baseless, :especially as, under any possible scheme of amalgamation, the ordinary share capital of the Salt Union would be sacrificed. This would be inevitable under the existing conditions of the trade. The situation is an unfortunate one for the shareholders of the Salt Union, but it would be a folly to ignore the facts of the case, and would be little short of criminal to allow the investing public, who are ignorant of the facts, to be misled by rumours such as these to which we have referred.

div.head: VALUABLE DISCOVERY. Science in the Colonies.
div.p: A VALUABLE DISCOVERY. Science in the Colonies.

Australia, the land of gold, has given to the world a great number of marvellous things, but the discovery made in that wonderful country by Mr Charles Forde,an eminent scientist and chemist, will probably do more good to mankind generally than all the gold venial Australia has ever produced. It is the discsvery of a natural vegetable substance which has the invalu- able property of acting in the process of diges- tion exactly in the same way as Nature's own animal substance bile. Now, since bile is necessary for the proper digestion of food and the continuance of a healthy state, and since interference with, and irre- gularities in, its secretion are responsible for most com- mon ailments, such as biliousness, indigestion, consti- pation, or chronic headache, it will at once be obvious what enormous importance attaches to a discovery of this kind. Mr. Forde quite realised this, and realising also what a boon it would be to the thousands who daily suffer from such ailments as those mentioned, he spared neither time nor expense in perfecting the preparation of a medicine in which his newly-discovered substance, while constituting the chief ingredient, should be supplemented by specially prepared curatives each of great healing value in par- denier directions. The substance so obtained was at last so concentrated, that a suitable dose could be con- tained in the space occupied by a small bean. It was then made up into the form of a bean which, being pre- pared for action on the bile, he called a Bean for the Bile. This name became gradually contracted to Bile Beans. The expense and care in per- fecting and compressing this preparation to the size of a small bean has been very great, but the result has been a small oval bean that the smallest child can take with ease, and a medicine that last year the consumption reached some thirty millions of doses in Australia alone, the rich and poor alike being the friends of this marvellous specific. the consumption to date has nearly baffled the best efforts of the proprietors their laboratories working night and day to meet the demand. Bile Beans have been found an undoubted cure for headache, biliousness, influenza, costiveness, piles, liver trouble, bad breath, rheumatism, indigestion, dizziness, buzzing in the head, fulness after eating, lack of ambition, debility, armnaia, female ailments, pimples, and a host of other ail- ments that owe their origin to defective bile flow assimilation and digestion. They will also be of great service in nervous disorders, loss of appetite, shortness of breath, blotches on the skin, insomnia, and troubled sleep. They act quickly in restoring females to health, and for a general aperient and tonic remedy they are almost unequalled. These Beaus are placed on the mar- ket in a form that anyone can take them without medi- cal supervision; and, as the price is so very low, there are few home e that cannot afford .to always have a box on the shelf for emergency. Depots and laboratories have been opened in England, and if you are unwell and a sufferer, and have doubts whether it is indigestion or not, the manufacturers invite you to write in to their London office, giving a full description of ailment, and free of charge you will be honestly answered whether Bile Beans will cure in your case or not. Address : The Bile Bean Manufacturing Co., 119 and 120, London Wall, London, E.e., and mark your letter " Special." You can also send to London if your dealer does not stock Bile Beans, and a box will be sent, post paid and packed free, on receipt of price, tbirteenpence halfpenny, and two and ninepence for large box (con- taining three times small size). There is only one genuine BILE BEANS, and that must necessarily have the name of the discoverer" CHARLES PORDE "attached.

Warrington Field Club.—Lecture on Snakes. At the second meeting of the session Councillor L. Greening gave a lecture on "Snakes; their Struc- ture and Habits," illustrated by a large number of beautiful coloured slides, which were shown through his lantern by Councillor Monks. Mr. ' Greening began by describing the snake's place in nature, the relations of this group of reptiles to the other great divisions of the animal kingdom. He then briefly touched upon the classification of the Ophidia, whose species he regarded as forming nine natural families; and proceeded to dilate upon the comparative anatomy, both of skeleton and internal organs, which not only presents many striking in- stances of adaptation to changing conditions of life and habitat, but proves the descent of all existing snakes from lizard-like ancestors. The development of the poison apparatus amongst the Elapine and Viperine groups, the brilliant yet protective colour- ing of many tropical species, and the modes of re- production were successfullydealt with in masterly fashion; whilst a few words on the geographical distribution of snnkes led up to the conclusion of a lecture which held the audience spellbound for over an hour. Dr White, the president, opened the dis- cussion, during which some of the theoretical ex- planations which Mr Greening had propounded came in for severe criticism; even those who dis- sented from his theories, however, joined with other members in warmly congratulating Mr Greening on his admirable lecture, and on the enthusiasm which he has always displayed in matter c, connected with natural history.

div.head: IMPROPER ELECTIONEERING.
div.p: IMPROPER ELECTIONEERING.
Strong Unionist Protest.
To THE EDITOR OF THE " WARRINGTON.

Sir,—l beg to enclose you extracts from an article that appeared in last Saturday's "Economist." This emphatic Unionist protest against the methods employed during the election is significant. And as the excitement of the contest subsides, one cannot but think that self-respecting and level-headed citizens, without distinction of Party, will begin to ask themselves whether on the one hand it is in the best, or indeed in any, sense of the word, patriotic to "exploit national feeling for partisan objects," or whether on the other hand, this is not just the way to drag down the whole tone of politics in future contests to a lower level. I therefore venture, with your permission, to draw the attention of those of your readers who have not previously noticed them, to.the pertinent and unanswerable criticisms of this Unionist Journal. _ .

div.head: Yours faithfully.
div.p: Yours faithfully.
A 11. CROSFIELD.

The following article appeared in the "Econo- mist" of Saturday, under the heading "Irresponsible Electioneering Talk" "England will scarcely look back with much pride on the general election of 1900. Sprung sud- denly upon the country, it has been marked by the lack of any real dividing issue, and by even more than the usual claptrap which popular electioneer- ing seems inevitably to generate. On one phase connected with this latter question we wish to say a word. There are few more baneful features of political strife than to seek to exploit national feeling for partisan objebts. History, to be sure, is full of such instances, but there is not a single case in which this thing has not wrought harm by engendering what the Greeks called " stasis," and which we might name by the word disruption. To tell you that you are a traitor and enemy of the country because you differ from me as to what is good for the country is to ifalsii'y issues, and to rouse the most dangerous kind of feel- ing. Many honest men have in the past been made traitors by such charges. In 1774 there was not a more loyal subject of the British Crown than Ben- ' jamin Franklin, but the outrageous abuse heaped on his head in the House of Lords converted him into the " rebel " in 1776, We do not, of course, say, or hint, that the abuse of the large number of people who do not admit the infalli- bility of the Gavernment will lead them into any anti-English policy. But we do say that to speak sneeringly and passionately of such persons as " traitors " and " pro-Boers." and to declare that any vote given to a Liberal or Labour canditate is a" vote given to a Boer" is to import a very bad and dangerous element into our political life. The I most extreme opponents of the war have opposed it because, in their judgment, it would injure the true interests of England. Such persons may his right or wrong, but, at least, their solemn assevera- tion has a claim to be respected, and their patriot- ism is at least entitled to as much credence as that of the Jameson raiders or the rowdies of the music-halls. If we are to accept the foolish catchwords uttered by passionate politicians given to " irresponsible frivolity," we must conclude that nearly half the country, though appealed to at a time of feverish sentiment, is composed of " traitors " and "pro- Boers." We were told that the country was united in favour of the Government. Why, then, appeal to it a year before the necessary time? When the appeal is made we were first told that any adverse or even hesitating response would instantly make a bad impression in foreign countries. And we were next told that every vote cast for a Liberal was a vote cast for a Boer. Considerably over a million votes have been cast under these circum- stances for Liberal and Labour candidates. Does any rational being, calmly thinking over the situa- tion, seriously assert that those who cast these votes are traitors ! The same abuse was heaped on those who opposed or criticised the Crimean War. What is the deliberate judgment of posterity on that ill-starred enterprise ? Is it not just possible that some historian of the next generation may say the same of some critics of the present war? Even though the critic may be wrong in the main, is not free criticism of the very essence of free institutions ? Is the critic to be barred out from public life ? Were that pos- sible, the free element in our institutions would not be worth many years' purchase, and the rule of the elected statesmen would give way to the rule of the soldier and bureaucrat. In a word, the in- nuendoes as to the " traitorous " character of those who have voted against the Government are ethi- cally false, and are made to look absurd in thelight of the election figures. "You cannot indict a whole nation, "said Burke. Nor can you charge half a nation " with being what you please to call " traitors " or "pro-Boers." Everybody will be ashamed of that nonsense in a few months' time. The absurdity of the accusation becomes the more apparent when it is seen that, roughly speak- ing, the Opposition presented no clear issue beyond that which the Ministry presented. The Ministers said in effect," We have practically conquered the Boers, and we mean, for the sake ot the future peace of South Africa, to annex their two States." The Opposition as a whole said, " We are not satisfied with the way you have con- ducted affairs, but after what has taken place we believe annexation to be inevitable." On what possible ground can the cry of traitor be used? in reference to the latter attitude? It is not a ques tion of individuals who put themselves in com- munication with Mr. Kruger or Mr. Steyn, but of the Opposition as a whole. Yet, "every vote given to a Liberal is a vote given to a Boer "—and that while Mr Morley himself accepts annexation as a necessary policy. It is impossible for us to con- demn too strongly such methods, which we hope will die out with the passing away of this not too dignified election. This is no party ques- tion, it concerns vitally the future of popular institutions. We are quite aware of the fact that, from one point :of view politics is a kind of game, and that much may be tolerated within the rules of the game. But among the things not to be tolerated are wholesale charges sought to be conveyed in meaningless catchwords concocted to tickle the ears of the groundlings. This sort of thing lowers public life and obscures all real political issues, Besides, as we have said, it lands us in ultimate absurdities, for it is impos- sible that half the people of a country can be traitors. If it were so, we should be on the very brink of revolution—but we are not.
Marriage .at .Daresbury Church.

The marriage took placcl on Tuesday afternoon at Daresbury Parish Church of Miss Margaret Dooley, second daughter of Mr James Dooley, of Hatton Lodge, Hatton, to Mr Thomas Hart, youngest son of Mr Thomas Hart, of Knipton, Leicestershire. The bride, together with her parents, is well known and highly respected in the village. The ceremony, which was witnessed by a large number of relatives and friends, was performed by the Rev Thomas Clarke, M.A. The bride who was charmingly attired in a dress of cream serge and hat to match, was given away by her father, and the bridesmaids were Miss L Dooley (sister of the bride), Miss Cissie Shepley, of Aston, and Miss llunbabin of Warring- ton. Mr J Hart (brother of the bridegroom), acted as best man. A reception was afterwards held at Hatton Lodge, where the happy couple were the re- cipients of the hearty congratulations of their friends. A large number of useful and costly presents have been received. Telephone 2339. Established 1849.

div.head: WARD.
div.p: WARD.
Result of the Poll.

The result of the by-election in Bewsey Ward on Mon- day was the return of Mr. Thomas Broomhall Malkin, the Liberal candidate, by a large majority. His oppon- ent Mr. Samuel Gough, the nominee of the Ratepayers and Property Owners' Association, fought the contest almost unaided. He had no committee rooms and very few workers. On the other hand, Mr. Malkin was well supported and several Conservatives also helped him. This was Mr.Malkin's third attempt to represent Bewsey Ward in the Council. A couple of years ago he tied with Councillor Rogers and upon a second poll taking place he was beaten by a small majority. Little interest was taken in the contest and the poll was an exceedingly light one. There were twe pollisg stati,ms, one at St. Ann's School, Dannett-street, and the other in Boyle-it. At the close of the poll, the ballot boxes were conveyed to the Town Hall where the voting papers were counted. The result was declared from the Town Hall steps as follows T. B. Malkin (L) S. Gough (I) 54

Majority 431. At the Liberal Club. After the declaration of the poll a large number of workers assembled in the Billiard Room of the Liberal Club. On entering the room, the returned candidate, Mr T B Malkin hid a hearty reception. Addressing the company, Mr Malkin said he felt very proud of the result. (Hear, hear.) He had fought for the third time and he thought it had paid for all. (Laughter.) It had meant a grea.t deal of hard work. It was not uatil Saturday evening that he received a copy of hie opponent's address and he was somewhat annoyed with one paragraph of it in which Mr Gough said that a man who was morally unseund was unfit for trust. He (Mr Malkin) net his opponent that morning and tackled him upon the question and they had some warm words he could tell them. (Laughter.) Mr Gough endeavoured to creep out of it by saying that he was not referring to him (Mr. Malkin) againet whom he had nothing to say, but against men who had seats on the Council. He (Mr. Malkin) then asked Mr. Gough why, if he meant that, had he:used the ward " man" on his address instead of the word" men." Mr. Gough said "You know as well as I who they are," which he (Mr. Malkin) considered a very unsatisfactory answer. Proceeding to refer to another part of Mr Gough's address, in which be spoke of Mr Malkin as a trades unionist being the nominee of a political party, Mr. Malkin said he had always been a trades unionist, but he also had a political creed which be did not sacrifice to anyone. He (Mr. Malkin) asked Mr Gough whether he had sacrificed his political principles on becoming a member of the Ratepayers' Association(—laughter)—and Mr. Gough replied that that was a different thing altogether. Before that meeting separated:he wished to thank all who had assisted him that day. He was pleased to think that he had the confidence of his fellow-workingmen. He had workingmen helping him that day who were true, straight and staunch and willing to do anything he bad asked them. To them he returned his hearty thanks. He also wished to tender his thanks to his Conservative friends who had worked so energetically on his behalf. He must especially mention Councillor Rogers who had worked hard for him (Mr. Malkin) and he was glad of tlx opportunity of thanking him publicly for his assis- tance. In conclusion, Mr. Malkin said as a member of the Board of Guardians for six years,he had endeavoured to look after workingmen's interests,and now as a mem- ber ot the Corporation he would work for them there and for the welfare of the town in general. (Applause.) Councillor Peacock having been asked to speak Mr. MALKIN said he believed Mr. Gough intended to oppose Mr Peacock in Orford Ward at the forthcoming November elections. (A Vice : " Let him come.") Be could aesure Mr Peacock that he would render him (Mr Peacock) any assistance he was able in the contest. Councillor Peacock said he did not know who was go- ing to he his opponent, but he thought he should have to begin and ask them what they were going to do for him. If he were beaten by Mr. Gough he should cer- tainly know that the ratepayers did not want his (Mr. Peacock's) services. During the three years he had been a member of the Council be had worked hard for the working classes. He was a workingman himself and knew what it was to be a workman as well as any min. He remembered on one occasion that a petition was brought before the Council to pre- vent Sunday burials. That, he considered, would have been an injustice to the working-classes as,it would have caused further loss of time and money on the pat of many working-people who could ill afford it. He opposed the proposed change and was severely criticised Iby the clergy for having done 80. He was a member of I the School Attendance Committee and he could assure them that that was a committee on which werkingmen like Mr Malkin were needed. A great number of working-people appeared before the Committee and they needed men there who would look at bcth sides of the question and:who realised the difficulties of working- people to keep their children at school. (Bear, hear.) There was one other matter be would like to mention. One:of the first acts he did on entering the Council was to agitate for the removal of the public convenience at Town's End. It was a great nuisance. He congratu- lated himself upon being the meats of having it re- moved. (Hear, hear.) He was not in favour of the political compromise, but in the event of him being opposed by an independent candidate he would ask them to rally round him and give him their support. (Applause.)
