div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY ON THE RAILWAY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE SHOCKING FATALITY ON THE RAILWAY AT WARRINGTON.

The Inquest. An inquiry was conducted at the Police Station Warrington, cn Monday evening, respecting the death of James Fox, a brakesman, on the London and North-Western Railway, who was knocked down and killed by an express train near the Folly- lane Bridge on Thursday afternoon whilst tempo- rarily carrying out the duties of lamp-lighter.—Mr Aspinall (stationmaster at Bank Quay) and Mr Mar- shall (locomotive foreman) represented the Railway Company. James Fox, 56, Napier-street, said the deceased ' was his son. He was 2:2 years of age. He (witness) was a brakesman on the railway. He last saw his son alive at ten o'clock on Thursday morning. He knew the place where he met his death. It was near to Folly-lane bridge on the up main fast line. He did not think that blame attached to anyone in the matter. He gathered that his son was crossing the line at, the time, and might have seen the signal for the express train had he looked. He was tem- porarily working as a lampman. His duties were to take the lamps out in the morning, trim them, and replace them at duak• The Coroner: There is no more danger in that than in the duties of a brakeaman ? Witness : No. - - - -

The foreman of the jury (Mr. Dale) said the de- ceased not having been conitantly employed at the work might have been thinking of his duties in- stead of the danger of the work. Witness said his son baLi done the work several times before.

Mr Aspinall observed that the deceased was an auxiliary brakesman and worked for other men while they were on their holidays. The Coroner: I suppose he would have been go • jag to light the lamps when the accident occurred., Mr Aspinall: He had some lamps on the other side of the line and would be crossing to them. He had been employmi on the line about eight years. Thomas Pierce, assistant in the signal depart- ment, said he saw the accident. He was on the north side of the Folly-lane bridge. He saw de- ceased starting to cross the lines, and when he was about to cross the down fast line, witness heard the whistle of the express. Deceased kept walking on , until he got on the up fast line. He then turned ' his head, and seeing the express made a dash for liberty. Witness thought he would have escaped, but the train was travelling too quickly. In answer to the Coroner, Witness said the signal would be to the right of the deceased. A Juror I suppose the express does:not usually whistle there ? Witness could not say. It might do because there was a curve there. Thomas Naylor, engine driver, said he was in charge of the Carlisle to London express on Thurs- day. The deceased was on the fireman's side, and the fireman used the whistle. Deceased when seen would not be more than a hundred yards away. The train was travelling at, the rate of 45 miles an hour. Witness saw the deceased after he was struck come out on his side. James Forster, the fireman, said he saw the de- ceased when about a hundred yards away.He opened the whistle and kept it open. Deceased seemed to realise the danger. Witness thought he would have got across. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death," and expressed their sympathy with Mr Fox, who had the misfortune to lose another son by drowning about fourteen months ago.

div.head: Application to the Railway Company for Market Tickets.
div.p: Application to the Railway Company for Market Tickets.

A quarterly Parish Council meeting for the parish ' of Dutton was held in the Board School on Monday evening, when there were present—Messrs Herbert Potts (vice-chairman, who took the chair in the absence of Mr Robert Fowles, chairman), Joseph Baxter, Peter Bunn, Abraham Blain, Thomas John- son, Thomas Wardle, and the Clerk (Mr Sydney E Stoke). Mr Potts propo-ed, Mr Wardle seconded, and it was carried that the Preston Brook, and Sutton Parish Councils, with the Anon Parish Meeting be asked to support the Dutton Parish Council in a petition to the London and North- Western Railway Company for cheap or market tickets from Preston Brook to Warrington, on Wed- nesdays and SaturdayE.

div.head: "WOMEN OF THE FRENCH REVOLUTION."
div.p: "WOMEN OF THE FRENCH REVOLUTION."

This was tbe subject of a highly interesting lecture which was delivered in the Bold-street Wesleyan School- room, under the auspices of the Wesley Guild, on Mon- day evening, by the Rev. Theodore Carrier, of Li verpool. There was a fair attendance, the chair baing occupied by Dr. Bennett. Mr Carrier is a most eloquent lecturer, having a splendid command of language at his disposal, and his hearers were kept deeply interested from start to finish of the lecture. The rev, gentleman at the out- set, said he was fairly familiar with tbe lives of the women who took part in the French Revolution, and it occurred to him that they would form a group of intensely interesting photographs, which would help mem to see the general aspects of tt e revolution under a somewhat new light. The lecturer then proceeded to recount the life of Madame Legros, and explained that it was chiefly through her action that the Bastile was stormed and destroyed. Ile graphically described the repeated escapes of Latude, who was imprispned in the tßastile . for having been imprudent enough to offend one of tha 'king's favourites. At length he was re-captured and confined in a cell below the earth from whence escape was impossible. He, however, contrived to drop a letter, written on linen with his own blood, into the street .and _ _

it was picked up by Madame Legros, who resolved there and then to devote herself to Latude's liberation. She went to the polica, bishops, ministers of State, and lastly to the kicg himself, but her pleading was in vain. She then told her tale to the people, and the nation was aroused. The matter grew into national excitement and the king's ministers advised the king to give Latude release, which he did. This clemency, however, came too late to appease the anger caused by the king's ob- stinacy. Madame Legros died a year or two before the de- struction of the Bastile but it was chiefly she who filled the French with horror and hatred of it. Madame De Stael's life was next touched upon and the lecturer spoke of the storming of the king's palace at Versailles by the womed insurgents who had become frenzied through want of bread, which could not be obtained owing to the prohibitive prices, arising from the heavy taxation of corn. The life of Madame Roland was also referred to and the lecturer spoke of her firmness of character. The murder of Marat by Charlotte Corday was the subject of a few remarks, and the rev. gentlemen concluded the lecture by a brief reference to the character of Marie Antoinette the ill- fated Queen of France. At the close he paid a eulogium to the faith, devotion and self-sacrifice,in which he said. women stood supreme. The male sex produced its dis- tinguished warriors, statesmen, authors, and its apostles and saints, but the female sex had produced its Grace Darlings and Florence Nightingales, and those who worked among the sick and poor, and thousands and tens of thousands of most dutiful, helpful,often wearied but never failing, English wives, sisters and mothers. These, no painter ever depicted on the canvas, and of them no poet ever sang, but they were the heroines of our life to-day and the angels of our homes. (Ap- plause.)—Votes of thanks to the lecturer and the Chair- man concluded the proceedings.

THE Liberal party The Danger of Parlia- mentary Groups. has always been a party , of groups,in some sense , or other. Any progressive party must consist of reformers wishful to press forward particular ob- jects, and seeking to educate Parliament with that end in view. The ballot, household suffrage in the counties, the burial of Nonconformists in parish Churchyards, and dozens of cther reforms, small and great, have been won by groups. We do not desire to see an end put to this method of advance and anybody who contends for unity, sameness, and perfect identity of views is no friend to pro- gress or to the Liberal party. There will be similar groups in the new Parliament, and they will do it no harm. But what there is some reason to fear is, thatdefinite parties may be formed, not to pro- mote single reforms or to advance a common idea, but to formulate a general policy and to act apart from ordinary leaders upon great occasions. If this progress is be carried out, of course there will be an end of leading in the usual isonse, and we shall see sections being led into different lobbies by their respective leaders, and the Liberal party, as such, will hardly have any existence. The past has furnished us with examples of the freest individual and sectional opinion, combined with perfect loyalty to a general leader, and that compact organisation without which no Opposition can be said to exist. The recent his- tory of the Irish party in the House of Commons has presented to us an instructive lesson iu the paralysing effect of hostile groups. The general election has wiped out distinctions in this parti- cular case,by reducing the ranks of the sections. It is:exactly what;would have to happen in the Liberal party if there were to be Parliamentary groups, with policies at variance with each other and incompatible with submission to a common leader. It would be necessary in the general interests of Liberalism, to make one policy possible by effacing persons and sections. But we have no fear of any such necessity arising. The general aims of Liberalism may be defined so as to prevent dis- unity, and they need not be pressed in a way to promote it. Liberalism is so essential to this country and its permanence as a progressive force in the world, that no disapprobation would be too great for the men who would destroy it,for the sake of a single idea. The Liberal-Unionists have set us an example of what happens when groups pro-
ceed to extremities. The Liberalism of the group has vanished, if the name has bean retained, and all its members are now as Conservative

are the persons who continue to describe them- selves by that name. The essential principles of Liberalism remain unchanged, whatever PeoPle may say to the contrary, and they are good enough for most persons. The Empire rests upon peace, and so do the commerca and prosperity ef the people. Extravagant expenditure may .t districts and classes, but it is demoralising, and 1 1 burdens the springs of industry, makes comPetl" tion more disastrous,and keeps down the working .° classes. If we have no reforms the Parliament machine works heavily, the Constitution ceases to be in accord with the times, and administration ls bad,corrupt and inefficient. Contentment springs, from the removal of grievances, the destruction et monopolies, the increase of equalities of opPertea nity. This country has to be democratised, as the only hope of saving it from amateurs in every branch of public life. Only the Liberal party ean do the work effectively, and if that be harapered,,' divided, and controlled by groups of independee; men and leaders, the continued ascendeneY .e, sham reformers, and clever wirepullers, and Pehtv cal bosses is absolutely certain.

It would give the belief that faith in the common sense of common people has not yet passed away, though the jury might demur to their title being thus ap- plied. As a matter of fact, the occasional eccen- tricities of juries at Assizes and Quarter Sessions have probably been the main cause for the reduc- tion of their services. Sometimes they display a most extraordinary desire to convict a man who is—at least in the legal sense—innocent of the charge laid against him; and sometimes they are moved by the discovery of one fault to find guilt as regards the indictment before them. Either in civil or criminal business there can be no question that a court of three judges would be securer than one of a judge and jury; but as that is too expensive, the present arrangement of considera- tion by one trained mind and twelve plain ones should not be lightly discarded.

The Wesleyan body lost one of its best men in the death of the Rev Charles Garrett, on Sunday. No man more earnestly devoted a long life to the public good than did the veteran temperance reformer and minister who is now being mourned so sincerely all over the country, and especially in Lancashire. The name of the Rev Charles Garrett has long been a household word in the County Palatine where he was beloved by all classes as few men ever live to be. In addition to being one of the most ardent teetotalers in the country he was equally as prominent a Methodist, and in 1882 received the highest distinction of the Wesleyan body by being elected its President, Liverpool particularly owes much of its advance from the lowest depths of impurity and intemper- ance to the work of Mr. Garrett. It is interesting to recall, in this connection, and as significant of the progress that has been made, that when he Went to Liverpool as pastor of Pitt-street Chapel, the basement of the chapel was sub-let as a spirit Store! The finest spirit store in Liverpool was on Wesleyan premises. A wag told Mr Garrett that be ought to be very happy with his enemy under his feet, but the rev, gentleman was not happy. "We set to work and expelled the spirits," he said. t was Mr Garrett's beast that he had never had an unkind word said to him in Liverpool, though he was out at all hours aLd mingled with all classes.

We wonder if Mr. Gough considers the support of some 50 voters sufficient to encourage him in his efforts to prevent better men than himself entering the Council. Such snubs as the one he received on Monday when Mr. Malkin polled 431 more votes would effectually quieten most men. But Mr. Gough seems irrepressible. We do not Want to question the motives of any man, but we Should like to ask Mr. Gough whether his pre- dominant idea is to get into the Council, or make things generally, and elections in particular, as expensive for the Corporation as possible. SD far his interfering methods have cost the town close Upon a thousand pounds. He may be proud of the fact, but if he is we can only hope that pride will, as usual, precede a fall—not necessarily off a house top but a fall of sufficient dimensions to hurt the faller. One of Mr. Gough's many incon- sistencies is to pose as a friend of the ratepayers and at the same time to take nearly a thousand pounds out of their pockets. Let them impress upon him still more emphatically their objection to such conduct and even Mr. Gough will be com- pelled to subside.

MATTERS OF MOMENT. -- A Provincial Letter. On all hands are witnessed preparations for wel- coming home from the war the gallant sons of proud parents fired with feelings of true patriotism at a time of national need. In one part of the country as in another Tommy will probably be treated much the same. Yet each locality will decide for itself how best to commemorate the achievements of the South African field forces of 'which the reservists and volunteers formed a part. Everywhere, and among all ranks, there is a desire to honour the men who have served Queen and country in an arduous campaign, and though the desire to kill the fatted calf may be universal and thoroughly appreciated by the " boys " themselves a permanent memorial would seem almost indis- pensable. The people of Norfolk propose to inaugur- ate a roll of honour, on which shall be inscribed the names of all East Anglican men, living or dead, who have served at the front. Happily the coun- try has few such wars, and therefore, each county or locality may contrive to do something that will serve to keep green the memory of those who have fallen and constitute a permanent reminder of the war that may now be considered virtually at an end.

Fac-simile Kruger sovereigns are being sold in some towns at a penny each, and the public need to be cautioned against receiving them as John Bull's. At Plymouth, a woman tendered one in a public-house, received change and was non est when the mistake had been discovered.

The Recorder for Birmingham takes a view of the right of prisoners committed for trial to with- hold their defence until tried, which is very differ- ent from the generally accepted idea. He told the grand jury at Quarter Sessions this week that he noticed it had become the habit of prisoners who had been committed, to decline to give evidence on oath before the magistrates, deferring it until brought before a jury. He thinks that if a person were desirous of giving true evidence he would give it at the first opportunity, and he expressed the startling opinion that the withholding of the explanation would have the effect of making the jury not inclined to attach importance to such prisoners' evidence. What appears to be new.to the Recorder in this instance is positively time- worn to other frequenters of the courts. Prisoners in electing to withhold their defence generally do so on the advice of their legal advocate, and some— times there are many good and substantial reasons for withholding the defence before the magistrates, particularly when it is known that the latter will not decide the case, and if trial by jury is worth anything, the prisoner who prefers that method is not only entitled to the supposed advantage, but has hitherto been credited with wisdom in preferr- ing it, and keeping" his own counsel" until he appears before the jury. It is perhaps worth noting that at the Recorder's court on the same day, a prisoner reminded the learned gentleman that he could not impose police supervision for attempted theft, and the Recorder had to acknowledge with a smile that the law from the dock was better than from the Bench in that case.

While one of the fashionable seaside resorts of Devon is exercised about cock—crowing as a nuis- ance, which it is endeavouring to suppress, another finds amusement in regular cock-crowing competi- tions. Cock-crowing cases have engaged the atten- tion of Torquay magistrates more than once, and been adjourned for one reason or another, without the question of whether it comes within the scope of a new by-law of theirs being decided. But the entertainment afforded at Exmouth by crowing competitions is of a very " decided ".character in- deed, and many prizes have been fairly won and duly awarded. The winning bird at the last com- petition crowed fifty times within the regulation half-hour, but another entertainment to be given last night (Friday) was to quite surpass in "public interest" all previous efforts. As some one has said, there is really no accounting for taste.

Boards of Guardians are as yet waiting for one another before deciding what course to take in re— spect to the Local Government's appeal for work- house dietary reform. The approval of the new tables by the " Board above "is not required, but the public would be glad to have an assurance that the committees appointed, and the medical officers of the various unions, had given the matter careful and diligent attention, for the sake of the children and the infirm especially.

The announcement that the National Lifeboat Association have provided a :new lifeboat of the "Liverpool pattern" for the deadly Manacles Coast, reminds one that nothing else has yet been done to save the navigation in that part, ot for Partly turning the dreaded dangers into a natural and friendly breakwater by mooring off the coast an up-to-date lightship. Several vessels have happily been warned off in time by the coastguard and others during the past twelve months, but what

may now be expected is that the authorities will continue to sleep soundly until there has been another serious loss of human life. As Pendeen Lighthouse is completed, it has been thought that the Elder Brethren might remember the Manacles lightship, and try to prevent another of these periodical holocausts. It is high time for something to be done in this direction, and it would be well if the London, Liverpool, and the shipping press were to sound an alarm before there is reason to regret not having done so.

Quite a number of cases of disease in various parts of the country have been diagnosed as malarial poisoning and attributed to the bites of mosquitoes. As most people are now aware, the insect carries the malarial virus in its proboscis, and the human being is in due course inoculated. Mosquitoes are by this time no strangers in England, and there are many persons, particularly in our seaports, who could tell of nights of misery, and subsequent days of pain, caused by these vicious visitors from tne tropics. It is not impossible that occasionally the common British gnat may be rendered bloodthirsty by an abnormally high temperature such as we had recently. But it is held by some reliable ento- mologists that there is no reason why the eastern pest should not find breeding and feeding ground in this country,, in the vicinity of docks and sluggish rivers. But, assuming that real mosquitoes did come and find the conditions favourable to lodg- ment here, the question arises, whence is the malarial virus derived? Malaria cannot exist ex- cept under frankly tropical conditions,and not even I then if sanitation properly asserts its sway.

Attention is once again being directed in the press of some of our large towns to the total in- adequacy of the periodical penalties imposed by the magistrates for suppressing the nuisance and the mischief caused by betting in the streets. The fine of £3 might operate as a deterrent on some classes of offenders; but the professional bookmaker steps lightly into the dock, and, knowing from experi- ence what the fine will be, planks down the amount sometimes before the decision is given, and goes forth with a cheery countenance to continue his illegitimate business. That his calling will be much affected by the strain of a "fiver" occasion- ally, in lieu of rent for the use of the public thoroughfares, it would be ridiculous to suppose. But this penalty is the maximum, and shows how , much an alteration of the law is needed.

div.head: HELSBY SEWERACIE.
div.p: HELSBY SEWERACIE.

_ A meeting of the Helsby Parochial Committee was held at the National Schools, on Monday October 15:h. Mr. James Taylor presiding.—Messrs H Bancroft and Son, Mancheeter, forwarded a letter with reference to their scheme for the sewerage.—Mr William Diggle, re- porting on the scheme, said on the whole he con- sidered the sewers were badly designed, and that the gradients were, in many eases, avouch too flat, and if constructed as designed, the sewers ere certain to cause great trouble to the district by accumulation of solids in the sewers which would cause continual stoppage and lead to the generation of poisonous emanations and gases, altogether detrimental to the health of the district. By this scheme the new sewer recently laid on land belonging to Messrs Guest and Blythe, and along the field in the occupation of the Helsby Athletic Club at a nett cost of £167 103 al would Ibe abandoned and consequently of no further use. For these reasons he could not recommend Mr Bancroft's scheme for the district.—lt was resolved that the report be adopted, and that the Clerk arrange for the necessary agreement to be entered into with Mr Dodd—lt was resolved that the clerk prepare a list of payment 3 to Mr Radford. in connection with the sewerage scheme and submit it to the next meeting.—On the ,question of the purchase of Helsby and District Waterworks being considered Mr James Taylor being a director of the Company retired from the chair and Mr White was thereupon appointed chairman of the meeting, when it was resolved that the matter be deferred and that the clerk ascertain from Mr Radford the number of gallons of water that would be required for flushing the sewers provided for in his scheme. The minutes were approved.

THE ALLEGED THELWALL NUISANCE Mr. R. A. Naylor wrote as follows to the Clerk under date October 22nd :—Dear Sir,—Yours of the 13th. In reply let me state that my last letters contain the truth and nothing but the truth. It may be hard to quietly submit to be called a liar, but I think my general zepu- tation will not bear this out. I notice Messrs Long and Son have already,in a letter to your Council charged your Medical Officer with duplicity, and so have saved me the trouble. Of course, your officials being entrusted with such positions show your Council consider them to be truthful, honest, 'honourable and sober, and fit and proper persons to discharge their obligations to the public, but there is such a mass of contradictions to be dealt with that letter- writing will not suffice. Admiral Jones-Parry has been addressing our Parish Council on the subject, and he states (quite rightly) the newspapers give the public a very erroneous idea of the matter. How can they do otherwise when such letters as mine of August 24th are not given to the reporters? Here are the closing remarks of report of samples of effluent men- tioned in m 7 last :—" The above aealyses snow Cha.7, these samples contain a large quantity of or- ganic matter of animal origin together with some tannin. They are v.3ry bad with a most offensive smell. The presence of free lime would tend to arrest advanced putrefactive changes for a short time, but these samples contain such a large amount of putriscible matter and their present condition is so bad that I am of opinion they certainly ought not to be run into any open sewer." Please note these samples were taken after filtration and were the essence of purity compared with what we bad when our coachman's children died through the smell. Don't you think it is almost time the cause of the nuisance should be ascer- tained. Probably the Yorkshire gentlemen who • invented the process might be induced to explain these modern methods of tanning to you. I will not trouble you; with all the cases of sickness which have occurred since your last meeting. Please allow me ta claim your valuable time to notice one. On Monday last a medical officer of health came here with a friend for the afternoon. Result—knocked down with the smell, lingered between life and death. Which was it to be? was the question indicated by the anxious looks of those around. Gentlemen of the Run- corn District Council I give you in one word this doctor's opinion of this nuisance—" murder."—Yours truly, R. A. Naylor. Mr. Clarke: Surely we are not guilty of murder are we? A Member: Yes ; every one of us. Mr. Linaker : Are we supposed to be a Coroner's jury. (Laughter.) The letter was laid on the table. DIPHTHERIA.

The Medical Officer -reported- a-case of diphtheria at Helsby. DEPORT OF VIE ALLEGED TANNERY NUIS&NCE. Mr. Farriogton reported that the instructions given at the last meeting in reference to the open ditch and out- falls to sewers on the side oi Waste-lane, in Grappenhall placed him in rather a peculiar position, as by such in- structions he was mailed upon to report upon the abate- ment, or otherwise of an alleged nuisance, which he never stated was,or reported upon, as being a nuisance. This may appear somewhat strange diction,but it is truc neverthelesi.—He however visited the spot on, the 11th and 22nd of the present month, and on those dates found nothing objectionable, therefore he considered that if the place was kept in the same condi- tion as it was in on the dates mentioned, the notiees served have been complied with; He granted that there was a tannery smell, and the liquid was discoloured, but as he had previously stated both these always did and always would exist wherever the trade and process of tanning was carried on :—On the 22nd instant he found I that Messrs Long had constructed a series of tanks on %hat was known as the upward and down- ward filtration system, and the tffleent pass- ing therefrom at the time of inspection ap- peared to be very satisfactory. He was informed that an inspector under the Mersey and Irwell Rivers' Pollution Committee had visited the promisterand had taken two samples of the effluent. These he presumed would be submitted tc Sir Henry Roscoe for analysis, and he was inclined to think that his report would be favourable. He ave-d with Admiral Parry's view (and always did from the first), rthst if the catchpit upon the side, and under the road !ma abolished, and the open ditch kept scoured ; or, better still, if piped under, all reasonable grounds for complaint would be done away with.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, OCTOBER 26, 1900 RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, OCTOBER 26, 1900 RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

ST. PAUL'S WESLEY GUILD. The young man's gymnasium in connection with this Guild op-ined for its sixth session last Monday evening. A large number presented themselves for membership. The members then took part in the following drills and ex,qc:ises :—dumb-bells, Indian clubs, bar bells, rings, trapeze, horizmital bar, parallel bars, parallel ladder, high jump, etc.

div.head: CHILDREN'S SUNDAY.
div.p: THE CHILDREN'S SUNDAY.

On Sunday at all the Wesleyan places of worship special services were held for the benefit of the youth of Methodism. The week previous had been set aside for intercession and prayer. At St. Paul's Church, Runcorn, the Rev. Alfred Wells delivered a sermon chiefly designed for young men and women. The results of the services were most satisfactory.

div.head: WOMAN MISSING AT RUNCORN,
div.p: A WOMAN MISSING AT RUNCORN,

On Monday the Runcorn police issued a notice to the effect that Lucy LiLtler, married woman, had been missing from her home, 48, Bentinck-st., Run- corn, since 830 p.m. on the 20th inst. Her descrip- tion is as follows:—Age 32 years; height, sft 3in ; light complexion, light hair, blue e 3 es, slenderlbuild supposed to he wearing a black three-quarter cape with hood. When she left home she:had in her pos- session a small basket with handle in centre and lid passing over it, and also a clasp purse containing about 103 in money. She has been in a depressed stat, of mini recently, and it is feared some ill has befallen tier. Oa Tuesday the Bridgewater Canal was dragged for a considerable distance, but with no result. Information may be given to Superin- tendent Pearson, Runcorn. WIDNES SUBSCRIPTION BAND AT FRODSRA.M.

The Town Hall, Frodsham, was on Wednesday night filled with a large and appreciative audience, the occasion being a grand concert in aid of the In- strumental Fund of the Widnes Subscription Band. The programme was capably sustained by the band. and the following artistes from Runcorn and Widnes :—Misscs Coward, Garvie and Hill, Messrs J Taylor (humorist), Stubbs (violinist), C Tem- parley and W Hopwood (vocalists), ad Mr Beckett (pianist).—Mr C Linaker, who presided, at the close of the concert said everyone present was thoroughly well pleased with the progra Mine they had hal the pleasure of hearing. The Widnes Sub- scription Ban i was deserving o:f every support if for no other reason, for their willingness in res- ponding to any charitable appeal that might be Made to them. Their performance that evening too had been excellent as was testified by the reception they got.—The artistes were repeatedly encored.— The proceeds of the concert proved very encourag- ing to the band, who were highly pleased at the manner in which the inhabitants of Runcorn flocked to their support. Mr W Byfield, drum- major of the band, had all the arrangements in hand and right well were they carried out. SOCIAL AT TN LIBERAL CLUB. Mr. A. R. Norman,J.P., presided on Tuesday night over a well-attended social gathering at the Run- corn Liberal Club. The meeting he described as an inaugural one of a series to be held during the winter for the purpose of e lucatiug members of the club in Liberal principles. Dealing with imperial- ism, Mr Norman, spoke of the Liberal party as the founders of the great colonies of which all were so proud; adding that had Liberals generally knovn the history of the British possessions, they would not have been iii any way affected by the " khaki issue." The musical portion of the programme was ably supported by Messrs W Shaw, E Kniveton, E Worrall. W F W Jones, T Yates, and W Booth, the latter of whom gave several suitable selections on the gramaphone. Messrs F Littler, W and I 0 Williams also contributed several recita- tions towards the evening's entertainment. The proceedings terminated wlth the "National Anthem" Next Tuesday Mr Colley, of Liverpooiiis expected.

div.head: THFC BURNING OF THE SHIP ROBY.
div.p: THFC BURNING OF THE SHIP ROBY.

A cablegram was received at Liverpool on Wednesday by Messrs R W Leyland and Co. to the effect that their ship Roby, which, as already re- ported, was abandoned off Monte Video on fire,had been completely gutted. The message stated that one boat's craw, consisting of the master (Captain Jones), the mite (Vaughan), and eleven seamen were picked up; but that nothing is known of the remainder of the crew. Cablegrams already pub- lished relating to the disaster spoke of fifteen men having been picked up by the steamer Santa Fe,and it is hoped that the further cable received on Wednesday night refers to the boat's craw which was formerly reported as missing. As the R3by carried a crew of twenty-seven or twenty-sight hands all told, this would acconnt for the whole on board. —it will be remenabarod that the " 13,3 by "

was one OF the ships lying off Runcorn during the strika at Runcorn Docks a short time ago. FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. R. E. B. BRUNDRIT. The mortal remains of the late Mr Reginald Ernest Barclay Brundrit, eldest son of the late Mr John Brundrit, of the Highlands, Runcorn, were in- terred at Runcorn Cemetery on Saturday afternoon. , The body was conveyed by road from Chester, and was met at Frodsham by the mourners, among whom were Messrs Percy and Cecil Brundrit (broth- ers of the deceased), Rev J J Bryant (uncle), Miss Barclay, Mrs Bryant, and Mr Brunirit (cousin). The cortege continued its way to Runcorn, and in Moughland lane it was joined by a number of prominent townsra,m, including Dr G Mc- Dougall, Messrs. G Hewitt, J Johnson, A Salkeld, John Littler, J S Davies, John Horsefield,3 a Weston, A Timmins,J Mort,Sergeant- Instructor Callaghan, M Barker, E Timmins and others. The bearers were Messrs J Turner, W Aspey A Aspey, J 8.11, W Harrop, T Ford, and C Williams (Chester). The body was borne into St. Michael's Church,where the first portion of the burial service was taken, the officiating clergy being the Ray. Thomas Me idows, MA, vicar of Thornton, Poulton- le-Fylde, and a cousin of the deceased. The solemn obsequies were finally concluded at the graveside. The coffin was literally enveloped with floral tributes from the sorrowing relatives and a large circle of personal friends. The deceased was 27 years of age.

div.head: RUNCORN HARRIERS.
div.p: RUNCORN HARRIERS.

The Runcorn Harriers entertained Farnworth Harriers at Ru ncorn on Saturday. Great interest was taken in the meeting of these teams, owing to the fact that the visitors are much stronger this season than they have been for several years. The general opinion was that Runcorn would receive a sound drubbing at the hands of their opponents, but the defeat was not so great as anticipated. The Farnworth men had their strongest team, while Runcorn were without four of their prominent run- ners, including W Thomas and S Hopkins. To this fact Runcorn attribute their defeat. A. good num- ber of runners took part in the race, the start being made at four o'clock. Trail was laid over seven miles of good country in the direction of Rock- saYage and Sutton, returning by Halewood home again. After a capital race home J Hosker (nor- thern champion) succeeded in gaining first honours, closely followed by W Lewis, of Runcorn. The fol- lowing were the positions of the teams ;—Farn- worth: 1, J Hogker ; 3, Handley ; 6, Broome; 8, Flynn ;9, Ratcliffe; total. 27 points. Runcorn: 2, W Lewis ;4, J Goodall ; 5, W Ray; 7. Stubbs; 10, Mathews; total, 23 points—a win for Farnworth by the narrow margin of one point. The race through- out was a good one, and certainly reflected great credit upon the Runcorn men. It prove 4 that if they combine they will be a thorn in the side of many first-class' clubs which are down to visit Run- corn this season.
ROYAL ARCII MASONRY IN CHRSHIRR,

A meeting of the Provincial Grand Chapter of Cheshire was held at Runcorn on Saturday, under the charter of the Bridgewater Chapter 753. The Provincial Grand Superintendent (the Ron. Alan de Tatton Egerton, NL.P.) and other officers opened the chapter, in one of the rooms of the Parish Church Schools, lent by the Rev CAnon Maitland Wood and the managers. There were companions presen t from Birkenhead, Chester, Altrincham, Hyde,Stock- port, Crewe, Knutsford, and Runco,n, the attend- ance being exceptionally good. The Provincial Grand Superintendent delivered an address, in which he alluded w th gratification t) the progress of Royal Arch Masonry in the province of Cheshire • IHe afterwards appointed his principal officers as follows :—Companion, F K Stevens-m, Birkenhead, as H; Companion Jame Wni ;e,Bridgewarer Chapter as J ; Companion William Hankinson, Bridgewater Chapter, as principal sojourn sr and Companion T H Annett, Bridgewater Cnapter as auditor., The Pro- vincial Grand Chapter voted sums of money to each of the local provincial charity institutions. After the Provincial Grand Chapter was closed, a large body of the companions adjourned to the Masonic Rooms in Devonshire Square, where a sumptuous high tea was much enjoyed. The usual loyal and masonic toaQts were proposed and duly honoured. The Grand Superintendent announced that the next Provincial Grand Chapter would be held at Birken- head. The thanks of the companions were accorded I to the various ladies who had ministered so admir- I ably to their creature comforts.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[By a Correspondent.] The mantle of his father may not have fallen upon Mr Herbert Gladstone, M.P., but he is recog- nised even by his opponents as a statesman; and in my opinion he never spoke truer words than those he gave ur.terance to at Leeds many months ago when he said that "Home Rule was dead." No party was ever more seriously split than was the Liberal Party by the late Mr Gladstone's proposal to give a separate Parliament to Ireland. Conscien- tiously believing he was in the right, the late Mr. Gladstone carried his point in the House of Com- mons,but failed to carry with him that break upon the chariot of progress the House of Lards. Events have marched rapidly during the last 15 years; ideas have changed; and when next there is a pro- posal to give Ireland a separate constitution it will only be in connection with the wide scheme of Imperial Federation. Home Rule, in the sense in which we know it, being now dead, there seems no reason why those Liberals describing themselves as Unionists should not return to the fold, and aid in carrying forward those principles of truth, righteousness, and liberty which are the foundation of the Liberal creed. It is with feelings like this that we welcome back into the family of Runcorn Radicalism, Mr Fred J Norman, J.P. Mr Norman may not see eye to eye in everything with which the Liberal Party is now concerned; but, it may with truth be said that in nine points out of ten he is in agreement with his old friends, and in regard to the Education Ques- tion, he is prepared to use the Americanism "to go 1 the whole hog." On this all important question, Norman has undertaken to enlighten the members of the Runcorn Liberal Club by a lecture, and his brother Mr Alfred Norman, J.P., at a social gathering at the Club, on Tuesday night announced that he had become willing to associate himself with the LibeTal party to this extent by the grossly unfair treatment meted out to Sir John Brunner during the recent contest. We welcome Mr Norman back into the ranks of Liberalism as an ardent educationalist; as a man of much local influence and powers in many directions; and trust that this is only the first step towards Mr Norman giving in his complete adhesion to the party which for generations past has been fighting might and main to uplift humanity.

Though the General Election is past and over, and the Division for the most part has settled down in its ordinary groove, certain local Tories take their defeat with very bad grace. What has caused their annoyance seems to be the utterances of Sir J. T. Brunner, M.P , at Davenham, and they are unani- mous in expressing the opinion, that had Sir John tutored them prior to the Election, he would have lost his seat. A likely story, and one which to a true Radical smatters somewhat of the" fairy tale series." On May Ist, 1900, Sir J. T. Brunner atten- ded the re-opening of the Runcorn Liberal Club.and in the course of an address delivered there (and surely that was before the Election), he said : "This war was said to be:inevitable ; and 83 many people had come to that conclusion, and the opinion had been expressed by persons so highly placed, that, it had come to ba almost a question of bad manners for one to express a contrary opinion. . . . . Peace was quite as inevitable as war. perhaps more inevitable than war. The war ought never to have been begun; but, now it had begun, peace was the inevitable end of it. . . . They (the Liberal Party) were not pleased with the enor- mous military expenditure which left us utterly unprepared for fignting 30,000 Baers in South Africa. Don't for a moment think that Cie Government was t 3 be held blameless for this state of affairs. If the war was inevitable they (the Government) were "fools and criminals" not to be ready for it."

Those were the utterances of Sir John in May last so that the "fancy" relating to his fear of uttering them before the election is nothing but a "fancy." I go farther, however, and maintain those were the expressed opinions of Mr Gladstone, Mr Mather, Mr Ellis Griffiths, and numberless others who from time to time appeared to support Sir John Brun- ner's candidature; an I, again, but for the fact, that the Conservative candidate narrowed the cmitest down to personalities, we would have heard more of those opinions, and had a larger dose of politics than the now disaffected Tories could assimilate.

In a Liverpool contemporary there is a letter from a " disgusted Liberal" the reading of which should make every Liberal disgusted, for it illu- strates that thP writer of it could not have followed Liberal politics, or the utterances of his own par- ticular Member —(Sir John T Brunner)—whom the writer swaggers about having voted for, for a con- siderable period—with any degree of attention. Let me suggest to the man, if he can honestly claim to be a true Liberal, "to go and reason with your neighbour," Have it out with Sir John face to face. Then if convinced of your unjustified atti- tude, be the man and apologise, if not let us all have the benefit of the interview. If,however,you are what I expect a " wolf in sheep's clothing,' afraid to sign your name,or afraid to reason with he whom you would condemn, then let it rest.

Now for something more domestic. In accord- ance with my policy of long ago, I now emphati- cally invite the Runcorn Urban District Council to make a bargain which will tend to the amelioration of the rates, and the lightening of the financial rez,- ponsibilities of the working-classes of Runcorn. At the special meeting on Thursday week the Coun- cil declared that 'the Transporter Bridge undertak- ing is likely to be a good investment." That, as will be remembered, was my first assertion. Having assured themselves on that point, they should go in for as many shares as possible. As yet, that has not been done. True, they intend to apply for £5,000 worth, but then, as is pointed out else- where, that will not carry any control. And control is really what Runcorn requires. That Lancashire will do little or nothing to assist is now assured for the Lancastrians—(Widnesians excepted)—are de- termined that the natural "door "between Cheshire and their own county is via Warrington. Hence, they will take no part in furthering the Transpor- ter Bridge undertaking. Finally let M 6 again urge , the Urban District Council of Runcorn to 1)1 cumspect, and being satisfied of the soundness of the concern accomplish such a stroke of business as will be beneficial to the town's posterity?

In another column will be found an interesting I article from the "Liverpool Journal of Commerce"on Salt Trade Rumours and realities. Et deals with the rumour that "a powerfal chemical manufacturing company" is likely to take up an invention in the salt trade which will probably cause a beneficial change in the process of manufacturing table or white salt, and points oat that such a rumour may be dismissed as baseless, especially as under any possible scheme of a.nalgamation,the ordinary share capital of the Salt Union would be sacrificed. The writer of the article ate° stateeit is perfectly oer• tam n that those who are most directly interested in the Salt Trade in Liverpool and Cheshire view it as a fabrication for share-dealing purposes," hence "it would be folly to ignore the facts of the case, and it would be little short of criminal to allow the in- vosting public, who are ignorant of the facts, to be I misled by rumours such as those," The article is I well-worth thoughtful perusal.

There has come to my ears what may be described as the Runcorn Cametery scandal, and with the ob- ject of getting it redressed I intend to fully inves- tigate the matter and give the Runcorn public the benefit of knowing the truth of what is now very much sub-rosa; My object in doing so is to fully prove that the" brief" I hold for the public shall be discharged fearlessly ; and at the same time give those who need it a timely warning. The results of my inquiries I shall publish in the form of an article.

div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.

Speech by Sir John Brunner M.P. On Saturday night Sir John T. Brunner M.P., paid a visit to Runcorn Liberal Club and although there bad not been any formal notice given of the fact, the large room was crowded te excess,and the passage was blocked to the door way. Mr. Walter Millington presided and amongst those present were Messrs. S Taylor J.P., A.R. Norman J.P., P B,Brimelow, Wesley Cooke, T Dean, T Lea, and f Wood. The Chairman in the course of an admirable speech, referred to the glorious history of the Liberal party,and said English politics had lately been showing a tendency towards Tammany Hall. We criticised American politics and the practice of giving the spoils to the victor, but the policy of the late government was :on the same lines for they had given spoils to those who voted in favour of a Tory government—the landlords and the parsons. (Applause.) Some time ago they had a fierce School Board contest in Runcorn and the battle was un- doubtedly won by the red herring of reduction of the rates. The people who made use of the cry had ap- peared on the Tory platform in support of Mr. Samson and in support of the government, which had given relief to voluntary schools. He challenged these gentlemen to deny that had the same relief been given to Board Schools the rates would have been reduced. (Applause.) But the Government gave relief only to voluntary schools. But there was even a worse case in connection wilts these doles and this was the sum of £78,000 ;voted in relief of rates on tithes. They would find that the average income of beneficed clergymen was £455 per annum and in their " poverty " they came cap in hand because they had assisted to put a Tory Government in power and each of these clergymen re- ceived a dole of £6 on the average. Was this fair? Did they hear of any other ministers than those of the rich- est church in Christendom receiving this money. It was for the men and women in the country to see jus- tice done and to vote and use their influence to prevent this sort of thing in future. (Applause.) Sir John Bruaner was received with loud cheering on rising. He said he expected to meet about a dozen or' two workers for a little friendly talk, and there they were as if they were in the middle of an election fight. He was delighted to find that the enthusiasm which grew and grew from the beginning to the end of the contest had not evaporated yet. He had had immense pleasure in listening to Mr Millington's speech. It was the sort of speech that they had not had in that consti- tuency for many a day, and he (Sir John) was bound to say that he took blame to himself in very large measure' for that fact. He had been invited into the constituency on so many non-political occasions that be had had a sort of feeling that he should be throwing the apple of discord into a community of people who were on such friendly terms with him if, as it seemed to him, he came down and took a side. But he had thrown that false sentiment of modesty entirely on one side—(applause)— and he meant between now and the next election to alter that attitude. Whether there would be a fight at the next General Election remained to be seen. It was promised after the declaration of the poll last Monday that there should boa fight, and Mr. Samson offered to come again if he was asked. (Laughter). Now, that was a saving clause. (A Voice: " His motor car would not bring him," and laughter.) If they were to read carefully what was said upon that occasion by his opponents they would see as c early as possible that the accusation about him (Sir John) being an enemy of Eagland was only a stick with which to beat a dog, and was never believed from one end of the division to the other. It was the old fight between Liberal and Tory. Taey hated having a Liberal representative, and what- ever means came to their hand to keep a Liberal out the would use them no matter of what character they were. It was not the first time he had heard of the intention of the members of that club—and he hoped of men outside that club—to start a new organization within the club for the serious study of politics, and he was heartily glad to know that such a project was in their minds, and he would do what he could te help it forward. He would come one Tuesday evening to speak upon the land question. (Hear, hear.) He recemmended them to ask Mr. Eiward McHugh to come and speak to them on the taxation of ground values. (A Voice : "He has premised.") That was a portion of the land question which he (Sir John) would deliberately leave to him. He would recommend them also to invite Sir William Bailey, of Salford, a director of the Ship Canal Compaay—(laughter)—and a very good Liberal. He came te speak for him at Wins- ford, and he delighted the people there. He was a man of enormous information, his reading was marvellously wide, he had dived into the very depths of all the corners of English literature. Since they last met he (Sir John) had issued an address to the electors about which he thought a good deal. New, there was nothing from the beginning to the end of that address in the way of formal thanks, but the spirit which breathed there was a spirit of thankfulness on his part for the work that was done for him and for the Liberal party. Never was a man so firmly supported and so stoutly backed as he had been and the Liberal cause had been at this election —(applause)—and he asked them to allow him;to tender them his heartfelt thanks for the work they had done. Mr Taylor had said that he was his (Sir John's) father, and that he was the father of all the rest • so Mr Taylor was their grandfather. (Laughter and a Voice ; " He's a good 'on.") He deeply appreciated what Mr Taylor and Mr Frith, the veterans amongst them, had done for the cause. There never was an elec- tion in which there was so much s:urdy hard work put into it as the one through which they had just emerged. He (the speaker) had been ashamed from time to time at seeing the sacrifice of time and the risks to health in- curred by Mr Taylor and Mr Frith, but he had consoled himself with the thought that, like him, they were work- ing for the principles that they held dear, and that it was not for him, but for the principles he represented that they had been working. (Applause.) He hoped their next fight would be a fight on politics—(hear, hear)—tod that the Conservative party might have as theireepresentative a gentleman who would strongly discourage personalities. At the end of last year and the beginning of this year he was very strongly opposed to the annexation of the two South African States. He sew fit to change his mind on that subject as most Englishmen did—as Lord Salisbury did. Last November Lord Salisbury said "we seek no gold fields ; we seek no territory." By the 30th May last, when he (Sir John) took the chair at the meeting in Liverpool, he had altered his opinion on that subject, and refused to go to the meeting un- less they would alter the resolution by striking out the protest against annexation. He was a practical poli- tician, and always was such. He altered his opinion for this reason—if they had not annexed these two States they would have pleased the Dutch, whom they had bitterly offended with a war that had been going on for a long time ; and if they had refrained from annexation they would have bitterly offended a large number of English people and people of British blood in South Africa. The policy refraining from annexation offered no hope of real peace, and, therefore, he changed his mind, and, would no longer protest against annexation. But on no other point had he changed his opinions, on no other point had he changed any declaration he had made. It had been said in a Conservative newspaper that during the contest he became an laa- perialist to win votes. He challenrd their recollection on the point. Dii not he say that he was an Imperialist if the Empire was to be Liberal, but if the Empire was to be Tory he wanted no Empire. He wanted the principles of liberty and freedom to spread the world over. That was what he meant by the extension of the British Empire. He did not want an extension of new territory to fill it with slaves. That would be a grievous blot uoon the history and character of this country. He could point them to a prospectus in which the officials of the Chartered Company told their shareholders they wanted black labour cheap in order to have cheap labour for their mining enterprises, and these blacks were to all intents and purpeses slaves in their employ. That was an extension of the Empire he did not want. He had not become an Imperialist in any other sense than that he desired the extension of &leash influence, because he believed that English influence was the highest and noblest in the world (Applause.) Whether in war or electioneering he (Sir John) neve: liked to drive his adverary to des- peration. Be liked to give his adversary a bridge to travel over, to get himself out of a difficulty, so that he might see fit to agree to what he wanted. Referring to the publication by Mr. Chamberlain of the letters written by Mr:John Ellie, Dr Clarke and Mr Lebouchere, Sir John said shortly before the end of the session Mr. Chamberlain told them in the House of Commons that there had been found in Pretoria letters written by English members of Parliament. He would not say what was in tbem, and he looked extremely solemn over it. He said he would a(-k the writer's permission to publish them, and he was apparently of opinion that if he asked under those circumstances to publish them he was at liberty to do so. He did net agree with that. These men daren't refuse permission to publish the letters. Mr Chamberlain knew that very well, and he absolutely compelled the men to say that they might be published. But that did not alter Mr. Chambneain's position in hs (Sir John's) eyes. He thought they all ought to have a regard for the sacredness of private correspondence as men of honour. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr Millington had reminded them that there was a fight upon the education question ctmine on be- fore very long in Runcorn. He would say a word upon the question of Education. He was always considered to be mad upon the subject of education. He repeated what he had said over and over again, that he wanted every boy and every girl to have the best possible oppor- tunity in youth of cultivating character and intelligence, so as to be able to use them in after life for their own advantage, for the advantage of their families and their country. He wanted that because he considered what he himself had enjoyed and profited by would not be toe good for anybody in this country. The highest possible education that a child could attain to would not he any too good for it. Let thrm all com- bine together to help the noorest child to the top of the trete (Applau He wanted that because he

/regarded it as a duty be owed to his neighbour. He was taught by his lather, when he was a boy, that he was to do unto others as he would they should do unto him; and there was no better way of trying to do this than by trying to secure fcr every child the opportunity of cultivating character and intellect. He wanted it for this reason—that in the long run men and nations got what they deserved, and he wanted the working people of this country to be better educated in order that they might get more wages. (Applause.) If they could only make every man in the country worth twice as much as he was to-day they would have all gain and no loss,and it was because he wanted England to beat all the world that he wanted England to be better educated. And because he wanted English people to rise in culture and to rise in comfort he was always hammering upon this subject of education. (Loud applause.) Sir John afterwards visited the billiard-room,and later left for Liverpool. Mr. R. H. Posnett also delivered a stirring address and after a little social talk the members ot the club and their friends dispersed.

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS. JOULE, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS. JOULE, OF RUNCORN.

Mrs. Joule, a lady well known to Runcornians by reason of her long connection with the Parish Church in the capacity of organist prior to the appointment of Mr J Johnson, at the advanced age of 76, passed away peacefully at her residence, 133, Greenway-road, on Saturday. A silver salver presented to the deceased in 1871, by the congregation of the Parish Church. bears testimony to the fact that up to that time she had filled the position of organist during a period of 34. years. She was greatly devoted to the church and church work in the parisn,and up to the time of her death she had evincedthe deepest interest in the preparations for the bazaar whin is being held this week in aid of St. Michael's Church organ fund. Her interest showed itself in an active cup- port of the enterprise by the collection of donations in money and kind. Her husnand ;was formerly a ship owner in Runcorn. He pre-deceased her Elortle years agosand another painful bereavement was the loss of her two sons. The family were held in high esteem in the town, and by the death of the subject of this notice the church has lost an earnest member and active worker. The interment took place on Tuesday atteraoon at Run- corn Cemetery, and was attended by the following : Messrs W Sutton, J Johnson, J Tudor. J Horsfield, M Barker, A Jordan, J Stokes, R Posnett, A Lightbarn, 1:1 Wdston who precedel the hearse. Dr McDougall, Mr F A Lake (solicitor), and Mr W E Rigby (West Kirby), followed. The first mourning coach contained Messrs J H Johnson (South Kensingtgn), H T Johnson (Horw;0), and L Bryan (Beckenham) ; the second con- tained, Messrs F R Cunliffe, and F Higgins (Rock Ferry); and the third coach, Messrs George Hewitt and W Crosby. The first part of the ceremony was carried out in St Michael's Church, Greenway-road, from wnence the cortege was led by the Rev Canon Wood (officiating minister) and the surpliced choir to ttie grave- side. Beautiful floral tributes of respect to the deceased lade were forwarded by the following : Mr and Mrs William Johnson, Mr and Mrs E L John- son, Mr and Mrs R T Johnson,Mr and Mrs J H Johnson, Mr and Mrs G Cunliffe, Mr and Mrs R F Cunliffe, Miss Cunliffe, Miss Johnson, Miss M Johnson, Miss Statham, Mr and Mrs Higgins, G U N and V Higgins Mr and Mrs Crosby, Mr and Mrs H W Nichols, Mr and Mrs T A Walker and family, Mr and Mrs Salkeld, Mr and Mrs J Tudor, Mr Harry Harrison, Nurse Ford, Mr Cecil Brun irit, Mr P Brundrit, Mrs Wardley, Mr and Mrs L Bryan, Miss Barclay, Miss Rongier, Mr and Mrs Poenett, Mr and Mrs Lake, Miss Smith, Dr and Mrs Raschen, Mr and Mrs Meadowcaft, Mr and Mrs Johnson (Runcorn), Revs r S Oliver and C P Bostiforth, Mr and Mrs A E Johnson, Mrs Woodward and family, Mr and Mrs William Cunliffe, Mr and Mrs Burrows, Mrs Whittaker, Mrs Tarvis, Mr and Mrs Banks, Mr and Mrs Stokes, Mr and Mrs Hewitt, Mr Statham. Mr R Morris, High- itreet. was :he undertaker. ••■•■•••111.000111P

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS-
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS-

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr M Williams, and there were present the members of the Rural District Council and Mr Robert Wright end Mr W E Gough (assistant clerk).

div.head: GUARDIANS AND THEIR DEPUTATION.
div.p: GUARDIANS AND THEIR DEPUTATION.

On the reading of the minutes of the last meeting Mr Limiter said at the last meeting in regard to depu- tations insinuations were thrown out about how many shilling cigars and shilling whiskies and sodas were in- cluded in the bill. He (lir Linaker), paid his own rail- way fare and for his own wine at dinner and took his own cigars with him. Remarks of that sort should not go forth to the public. Mr Turner said he also paid his own expenses. Mr. Mclntyre suggested that they had better treat the remarks with contempt. Mr Linker said that was what they deserved, but since the report appeared in the newspaper he had been twitted with the remark " That i 3 bow you go oh." He did not think it was fair for people to give their time and spend their money and then have remarks of that sort made. The Cnairm%n sgi3 he had attended on more deputa- tions, conferences Szo., than anv member of the Board and he had never come back home without being out of po3ket. He thought members of deputltions were en- titled to be as well housed and as well fed as they would in their own home, but beyond that luxuries had never bean charged. 4Mr. Woodward 'illbore testimony that the utmo,st ' economy was practiced by deputations. When- ever he had acted he had never come home as good a man financially as he went. They would always have grumblers, but ne was glad that most of their consti- tuents were of opinion that deputations should be treated in a proper manner. Mr. Turner: May I ask who the grumblers are?

(Applause.) Mr. Wright said he attenied the Health Congress at Aberdeen with the Chairman of the District Council and the Clerk,and nothing was paid for by the Union except orainary hotel expenses. They paid for their owns wine and cigars and other luxuries oat of their own pockets. The discussion then oaased. PEOVISION FOR EPILEPTICS WANTED.

A letter was read from Mr J E S Olive clerk to the Wirral Union ioquiring what arrangements had been made by the Union for the treatment of other epileptic cases. At present his Board had a boy. 12 years of age in the Workhouse who was an epileptic, and was reported by the Medical Officer to be dangerous. Ho recommended that the boy should bs removed from the workhouse and placed in a home. The only home his Board knew of was that at Maghull, which was always full, and always had a long list of cases waiting for a vacancy. Ueder these circumstances it was not avail- able except perhaps after a long period of waiting, for odd cases such as occur in a Rural Union ; and he was directed to write to the other anions in the county, with the view of ascertaining whether any of them had made any special provision for such cases which might also be available for other unions, and if not, whether they did not think it desirable that all should unite to provide such a home for the county. The Chairman said the only reply was that Runcorn had no provision for epileptics, and the Board could scarcely take the initiative.

div.head: ASYLUM CHARGES.
div.p: ASYLUM CHARGES.

Mr. 1. Hornby, clerk to the Visiting Committee of the Chester Asylum, wrote informing the Board that at a meeting of the committee, the rate of ms.intenance of pauper lunntics in that asylum fo the quarter ending December 31st next, was fixed at 7s 10i1 per head per we.k. Mr. Hough said this was an advance of 311 per week.

div.head: POOH LAW ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE POOH LAW ASSOCIATION.

Mr. H. E Ltwrenc, secretary of the Association of Poor Law Unions forwarded a circular giving notice that the second annual general meeting of the kssocia- tion would hP held in London on Thursday and Priday, Nov !tuber 15% and 16'.,h, 1900. 00 the motion of Mr Wright it was decided that the Board be not represented at this conference.

div.head: BOY BADLY BITTEN.
div.p: A BOY BADLY BITTEN.

John Ditchftsid, aged 11 years, whe resides with his parents at Penketh-lane, Runcorn, was on Tues- day night very badly bitten on the right arm, by a dog. He was attended by Dr McDougall and is now on the way, to recovery. It appeared the boy was playing with several others about the street, when the d3g,who is supposed to belong to a Widnes man, rushed up and snapped a piece out of the little fellow's arm.

div.head: Good Templary.
div.p: Good Templary.

The "Young Mission of Warrington" Juvenile Temple held its weekly meeting on Wednesday in the Brick-street schoolroom. Sister S L Sheath, C T, presided,and ten 'new members were initiated. Sister Mrs Sheath, SJ T read the quarterly circular of the Grand S J T, Bro J W Hopkins (Gloucester) Mr Jenkins formerly a member of the "Bonehill Branch" Lodge, Latchford, gave a brief address. Bro T Jackson gave a recitation, and Sister Sheath sang ''Joe Perkins." The weekly meeting of the Temperance Mission Lodge was afterwards held in the same room. Bro Roberts presided, visitors be- ' ing present from the "Star of the East" Lodge. Bro J Sheath reported having visited the "Concilio et Labore" Lodge, Manchester. The programme for the evening was "half-pound night" and re- freshments were handed round. The following programme was given:—Bro Litherland, song, "I have no home," Sister Dillon, song, "Sweet Gen- evieve," Bro Dillon song,"Qaeen of the Earth" Bro O'Brien moved that the best thanks of the Lodge be given to the visitors, Sister Sheath,sen, seconded and the resolution was carried. Bro Dillon re- sponded, after which the lodge was closed.

THE TRANSPORTER BRIDGE FOR RUNCORN.
Runcorn Decide to Invest

div.head: Why Not £10,000?
div.p: Why Not £10,000?

&low we print a report of a special meeting of the Runcorn Urban District Council, at which a resolution deciding to invest £5,000 in the proposed transporter bridge acrobs the Mersey was carried with three dissen- tients. We understand, h4wever, that the capital of the company will be £lOO,OOO with a directorship of nine and that interests of less than £lO,OOO are not likely to carry any control. The only object Runcorn can have in an investment of this kind is obviously one where they would at least have some voice in the con- trol of affairs ; and since the majority of the Council are agreed that the investment will be a sound and judicious one, why not invest £lO,OOO and obtain some control ? If "£5,000 without control "is good; surely "£lO,OOO with control " will be a far better investment. Let us urge the Council to reconsider its decision at an early date, and inveit tbe larger amount.
SPECIAL DIEETING OF THE iIIIINCORN URBAN DISTRICT
COUNCIL.

Oa Thursday evening a special meeting of the Run. epra Urban Council was held for the purpose of deciding the question of taking up shares in the Transporter Bridge Company. Mr Haw:lvry prosideLl, and there were present.—Messrs S Taylor, D Bisbrown, M J Sweetman, T Junes, J H Salkeld, ti Hewitt, F

James Pritchard, R II Posnett, h Gatley, GB Kirkham., J Wilbon J U .; rx, I' Dean, I? A bake, (law clerk), E Marslaall (secretary and accountant), and James Wild. ing (surveyor). The question having been debated at great length by

the Council and Committee, _ _ Mr S TAYLOR moved the following resolution .—" That the Council contribute t 3 the undertaking of the Corn. pany constituted for the construction of tne transporter bridge under the provisions of the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Act, 1900, the sum of £5,000 in shares in the said Company, on condition that the Local Government Board permit tee borrowing of the said sum and tne repayment there- of within a period of not less than 30 years ; that the Company pay interest on tie amount paid during the period of construction; that toe Ceuncil nave power to appoint one director or ties Company; and that the ne- cessary agreements be entered into." Mr Taylor thought they must all agree that this undertaking would benefit Runcorn to a very great extent. He was sure they would have the support of the public in what they were deciding upon that night, Ile tnoroughly believed that the undertaking would be a profitable one—he failed to see how it could be anything else—and if they had £5,000 invested in it he would look forwsrd to a profit- able return, which could go towards easing the rates. He could not but think that it would be a good invest- ment, and that the bridge would be a great boon to the people of Runcorn. Mr. Pritchard seconded. He thought this was a scheme which would undoubtedly benefit Runcorn and the community on the other side of the water. It would be the means of increasing trade and traffic between two important communities, It would materially ad- vance the interests offboth, and in making this invest- ment he thought they ran very little risk whatever. In his opinion they would receive in the form of interest upon it suffizient to pay for the borrowed capital and the annual instalment, so that the £5,000 would be a capital expenditure which would be obtained from that Council without any cost, he thought,to the community. There was no doubt that the farm produce of Cheshire would be introduced to Runcorn and to Widnes, and that there would be a considerable increase in the traffic between the two places. Mr. Posnett supported. He was so much in favour of this bridge, and so much in favour of the future of it being of the greatest advantage to their town, that he thought one of the greatest pleasures that their Chairman would have to look back upon, was his asso- ciation in the chair of the Council, in favour of Runcorn taking an interest in this undertaking. He believed they would be able to look back upon their action that evening as being a good stroke of work for their Own. As long as be had been in Runcorn he had felt certain of this, that in every important point they could work to- gether with Widnes for mutual advantage they were working for the distinct advantage of their own town. He was sure that whatever they could do to increase competition with the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, and to increase the facilities for getting in and out of their town, wouid be to the advantage of , Runcorn. He did not think there was the slightest possible chance of creating an additional charge upon the rates; he believed the amount of the contribution would be more than recouped. They would find there would be a considerable difference in their-railway rates between Runcorn and the other side of the river, when there was open competition along the Transporter Bridge.lt was for this very reason that the Warrington Corporation had looked askance at the present scheme. The traffic across the Warrington bridge was enormous, and the Corporation had had a number of schemes before them—and they had one under consideration at the present time—for the widening of their bridge so as to provide better facilities. It they could get this Trans- porter Bridge he (Mr Posnett) thaugnt they would get a _ _ _ _
reat deal a the traffic now going round by Warridgtoa
—for instance the traffie bkwe&l Runcorn and St. Helens. He believed they could get 99 per cent. of that

traffic across the new bridge, There we the further question as to who should supply the power for this bridge, and be would like that Council to do all they could for their own town in taking shares with this Com- pany, so as to use all the influence they could to get the motive power on the Cheshire side of the river. If they declined to take shares in the company they had no locus standi ; and they had no authority in the Councils , of the Company ; but if they:showed their interest in the ' concern he believed that the company would do its best for the town. He (the speaker) lallieved this was one or the grandest schemes for helping Runcorn that they had ever had before them, and he only regretted that their proposition was not to invest £lO,OOO instead of £5,001 Mr Grice said he thought to oppose such a scheme as this would be like committing social suicide. Mr. VI isw all said he was not prepared to contribute £5,000 towards this scheme. He could not agree with Mr. Posnett that it was one of the grandest schrenes that had been brought forward. The vehicular bridge scheme which they considered some time ago was a far better scheme than the present one. (Mr Posnett : Where is it.) Mr Wiswall, continuing, said the proposed Transporter Bridge was not a bridge in the true sense of the word. It was only a sort of ferry in the air across the water, and it was only a single line. His fear was that it would block the way to a better bridge when the proper time came. Mr. Wilson said there was something in the scheme which must impress every one of them with the import- ance of having a representative on the board of direc- tors, to 803 that their interests were fairly safeguarded at the proper time. He did not think £5,000 was a suffi- cient sum for the ratepayers of Runcorn to invest in the scheme. If it was a good thiog why hesitate? Why not go in for a sum that would fairly benefit the rates ? If it was as good a thing as had been represented, a substantial sum invested in the undertaking would re- lieve the burden of the ratepayers who, at the present Imoment were paying as much as they cared to pay or more.

Mr Imison dissented from Mr Wilson's Ifttter remarks. He (Mr Imison) would support the investment of £5,000 on this ground—he thought the ratepayers would be quite prepared to secure the impr ived slight risk to them. Taken at its worst the investment of .415,000 could only mean, assuming that there was no income, an increase on the rates of something like lid in the £; and, so far as his judgement went. the ratepayers would be prepared to risk that. Mr El,lan believed that as far as Runcorn was con- cerned the scheme would be a great advantage, and he did not see what was to prevent their town from becem hog a regular centre for agricultural produce. Most of the agricultural produce at present went to Warrington,and Widnes draw its supply chiefly from Warrington. Ile did not think they had to itretch their imaginatien very far to convince themselves that Runcorn might become the market centre for the agricultural produce of Ches- hire and that Widnes could be more easily supplied from Runcorn than Warrington. Mr Bisbrown thought they would regret it if they took a hostile attitude on a proposition ot this kind. Mr Taylor, replying on the discussion, said they were all agreed that a permanent vehicular bridge would have been very much better, but were the Runcorn and Wid nes people to wait another 50 years for communicdion between the two towns? The resolution was then put and carried. Messrs Hewitt, Wiswall, and Kirkman voted against it.

The North Cheshire Hunt. On Wednesday the North Cheshires kept tryst at Daresbury and did capital work, including a good hour's hunt. Daresbury Firs were well populated with Albs, and the hounds bustled them about merrily and chopped one in the cover. The Owl's Nest was next visited, and a fox broke into the open, ran well to Newton Gorse, thence on to Grimsditch, and made a ring to Rosewood, Dares- bury. There were a few checks, but the hunt lasted an hour and was most enjoyable. Warrington Markets. At the Warrington Corn Market on Wednesday new wheat fetched 38 6d to 38 9d (701 b to the bushel) ; new oats, 28 21 to 28 31; old oats' 2s lid; flour, best seconds, par 210Ib, 21i ; bran 11 1 per 201 b.
