div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

SEQUEL To THE THEFT OF A HORSE CLOTH. On Friday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court before the Mayor and other inagistreees, Georee Burst, 22, Bank•street and Thomas; Birchen, 82, Chuseh street were charged with stealing from the vaults of the Manx Arms, School Brow, on Tuesday afternoon a horse cloth value 155., the pro- perty of Isaac Swindells. Birchen was further charged with assaulting Detective Meacock whilst in the • execution of his duty, and Joseph Birchen, brother of ehe accused, was charged with assaulting P.C. Penning- on at the same time and place.—Mr Browne defended— Detective Superintendent Monaghan detailed the facts of the case to the Bench. It appears that on Tuesday afternoon, Swindells went with a friend to the Manx Arms. He had a horse-cloth in his possession and be laid it down on the seat. Hurst and Birchen were in the vaults at the time,and shortly aces- wards the horse-cloth was missed. Inquiries were made by Swindells, and he wee told that gurst had been seen taking it away. Hurst again entered the Mena Arms, and Swindells charged him with taking the cloth, but he denied all kaowledge of it and protested his innocence. The police were informed and on visiting a public-house in Cnurch-street, the three defendants were seen toget- her drinking. Detective Meacock called Hurst aside and took him to the police station. From a statement made, Detective Meacock proceeded in company with P.C. Pennington to the business premises of Mr. Birchall, the father of the defendants. fle there found the horse cloth on a shelf. Whilst talking to Mr Birchall, Thomas Birchall came into the shop and tried to teke the horse-cloth from Detective Meacock, stating that it was his property and that he had bought it. He then struck tne officer a blow on the chin with a clasped knife. P.C. Pennington got hold of Thomas Birchall and a severe struggle took place. Whilst struggling to get the prisoner out, Joseph Birchen, a cripple, came on the scene, and with his crutch struck P.C. Penningten in the chest. Thomas also struck at Detective Meacoek, and in the scuffle the detective's hat was damaged. Thomas was eventually got to the Police Station, and the officers returned fos Joseph. He again struck out with his crutch, and asked his father to gat a gun and shoot the officers. The prisoners had had drink at the time but knew what they were doing.—Evidence bearing out these facts was given by Isaac Swindells,Thnmas Edmonds. James Cairni,Detc- tive Meacock, P.C. Pennington and P.C. Clough. Cairns stated that Hurst told him he was going to "nalf-inch ' the horse cloth,an expression which Detective Menagshan said was a slants term meaning " pinching "at taking it.—For the defence, Mr Browne said this was a lament- able case and arose through drinkine. Hurst and Thomas Birchall were in the Manx Arms whed Swindells entered and they commeecse e argaining for the horse cloth, and Birchen was ender she imoreesion that he bought the horse cloth. Mr Swindells had ad- mitted that Birchen was offering to ouy it. It was a difficult matter to decide where the belief in a purchase ended and where felony began. Birchall was a per- fectly respectable man and be could only account fer the il!-treatment of the officers as being due to uncontrollable temper. With reeard to Joseph Birchall he also lost his temper in consequence of his brother being locked op, as he was under the impression that his brother had bought the horse cloth.—The Mayor said the Bench had decided to fine Hurst 10s. including costs. The charge of theft against Thomas Birchall was dismissed but he would be fined 403. and costs (£2 15s) for the assault on'the police, and Joseph Birchall 203 and costs (£1 193 6d). The magistrates asked him to say that while they did not think that Thomas Birchall appzeciated the fact that ha bad a knife in his hand it might have resulted in a serious charge being preferred against him. A SUNDAY VISIT TO WARRINGI.3S.—DISGRACEFUL CONDUCT. T. B. Brown and Michael Ksrnari, two young men living at Hartford, wete arraigned in the dock at the Borough Police Court, on Friday, as the result of their conduct in Longford-street whilst on a visit to Waning- tort on Sunday, the 4th inst. Kernan was charged with assaulting Susan Hanledine, a married woman. of 140, Longford-street, and Brown waa charged with Committ- ing a use offence on Fanny Appleton, who lives at the same address.—The complainants reside at a shop in Longford-street. and on the Sunday afternoon in ques- tion they were sitting reading in the house when they were surprised to see the prisoners, who were complete strangers, walk through the shop and enter the house. They then sat round the fire and commenced to smoke and spit about the place. Mrs Flastedine and Miss Apple- ton protested, and asked them to leave the house. They refused to do so, and Mrs Hasletline then told them that her husband was ill and that if he became upset it might be a serious matter. She again asked them to leave and said if they did so they would bear no more abont it. The defendants nommenced to use abusive and foul language. Mr. Hasledine then came upon the scene and ordered the stringers out of the house. Kernan then struck him in the stomach, and also turned upon Mrs flasledine. whom he struck on the shoulder. Brown got hold of Miss Appleton and smacked her face and otherwise assaulted her. He then asked her to think of him as a brother and not as a stranger. Eventually the defendants were got out of the hense and later in the day Brown was seen near the Horse and Jockey in his shirt sleeves challenging to fight any man in Lancashire. The Mayor said the magistrates were of opinion that it was about as unique a case as they had heard. Person- ally he had never heard anything like it in that court It was an absolutely unwarranted and unprovoked assault, and it would have served the defendants If they had met some big fellow who was able to take it out of the pair of them. They would be each fiaed 203 and 104 costs ; or in default one month's imprisonment. SEW:EL TO A SHOOTING CASE.

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, Arthur Jones, 44, Hume-street, was summoned for earrying a pistol withcut a licence on thc 27th Soptember —Mr May, who prosecuted on behalf of the Inland Revenue, said the defendant was before the Court on the Ist inst. on a charge of shootin,g a servant girl in Bridge-street with a pistol and it was stated then by the Chairman that the Inland Revenue would probably proeecute him for carrying the gun 'without a Hoare. The prophecy had come true, but he had been directed to sate that the Board did not desire to prom for a heavy penalty. The proceedings had been taken mainly with a view to suppressing the increuing use of pistols and revolvers. It was, however, his duty La ask for a penalty so that the finances nf the county borough might not suffer by the case.—P.C. Turner des- cribed the circumstances of the ease and defendant was fined 103.

' Hannah Jackson, 6, Plumpton-street, were charged with neglecting their five children on the 12th October in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health. They p'eaded not guilty.—Mr.Browne. 1 who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., stated that 1 the male prisoner was in receipt of good wages—averag- ing 29; per week. Out of that he generally gave his wife £l. and spent the rest in the usual way. During the last few months they had lived in five houses, each of which they left in a most filthy condLion. The case had been under the observation of Inspector Hackett since May, 1899, and he would have prosecuted in August but the prisoners suddenly disappeared. Shortly afterwards they were found but the Inspector had so r much other work to do in the district that their case ' was left for a time. Two inspectors were really needed in this district, a fact which had been lately admitted by Mr Lee, the local hon. secretary of the society. On the 12th inst P.Q. ,Woods again reported this case to the Inspector, who in ' company with Woods visited the house that night. They found four of the children alone in the house, two of them, who were half naked, being on the door step. The night was very cold and the chil- dren were almost starved. The prisoners were out. Nellie and Edward, two of the children, aged four and three respectively, were asleep on a wooden sofa. John, aged ten, was very poorly clad, poorly nourished, but fairly clean, while James was fairly well clothed, but was badly bitten with vermin. Nellie was half naked, filthily dirty, badly bitten with vermin, and her shoes were completely worn out. Edward was also half naked, the clothing was filthily dirty, his body was clean but badly bitten, and he had no shoes or stock- i lings. There was no light, fire or food in the house. I and the neighbours had given the children food.— P.C. Woods gave evidence bearing out the above state- ment. He said he had warned the man. The neigh- bours were constantly complaining about the shocking condition of the house.—Sergeant Evans spoke to. visit- ing the house in May ef last year. It was then, he said in a very bad state.—John William Smith, County Court bailiff, said that in April he visited the house in order to see the man about a debt. He went upstairs, but had ta rush down into the yard owing to the abominable, smell. It made him ill. The children were then run- ning about naked. He informed Inspector Hackett of the case.—lnspector Hackett gave corroborative evidence. Be added that the beds were broken down, and were very filthy. The stairs were ,black with dirt and the dust on the bedroom floors was about an inch and a half thick. Be stayed at the house nearly an hour but neither of the prisoners came in. He asked P.C. Wocds to watch them. Both prisoners were to blame for the neglect.—Superintendent Monaghan stated that that was the male prisoner's seventh appearance. The prisoners were sent to gaol for three months.

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society— Open Meeting. .

Wycliffe Church was well filled on Sunday afternoon, on the occasion of the open meeting of the P.S.A. Society when the proceedings were thrown open to both sexes. The President (Rev J Yonge), occupied the chair, and in the course ot a short address, he said he knew there were many men in the town who were thankful that the P.S.A. meetings were ever begun, and he was sure that if they were thankful the wives at home were thankful too. (Bear, hear.) He was glad to think that the society had been the MEMO of brightening and Christianising many a home in Warrinetoa ; lifting it out of the darkness, sorrow, gloom and unhappiness of sin and introducing a peace, rest, light and joy, which it was stranger to before. These were things they were bound i j think of and take courage.Be hoped they would still go on being useful and that would be tlr, 2reat justi- fication forlthe existence of the society. In introducing Mr J W Tharme of Liverpool, as the speaker;the chair man said Mr Tharme's late father was well known in the town in connection with the Railway Mission for which he did great service many years ago. Mr Tharme re- ferred to the pleasure it gave him to visit Warrington and address some of those who bad listened ta his father's voice. He proceeded to speak on the subject "When is a nation safe" During the last twelve months he said a great deal had been written and spoken about the safety of the English nation. It was urged that by increasing our army and adding to orr navy we were to gin prestige, safety and security. He proceeded to show that that nation was safest which trusted in God, and walked in the ways of God. We should never, feel safe until we allied ourselves with God through Christ. An attractive musical programme had been arranged and was creditably given by the Wycliffe Choir under the conductorship of Mr il H Payton Mus Bac. Amontzst the items given were the anthems "Sing to the Lerd" and "Abide with me," the solo parts be ing taken very efficiently by Mrs R H Pearson, Mr A Grif- fiths and Mr W H Wallington.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY OCTOBER 26, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY OCTOBER 26, 1900.
HALTON COURT LEET.

On Saturday there was held the annual meeting of the Court beet for the manor of Halton. The gathering took place in the courtroom of Halton Castle, which now forms part of the hotel erected on the site of the original gateway. Unfortunately the high steward, Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, was arable to be present 1 and the deputy steward, Mr. Kirkconnell, officiated in his stead. The quaint ceremonial of olden times was carried out in due form. Warrants had been seat to those qualified bathe wide area over which toe court now holds sway, in name if not in fact. The attendance was, however, not up to the average. The bailiff, Mr. Walker, made the usual proclamation from the entrance to the court. All who " owe suit and service to the court" were commanded to "draw near, give your. attendance, and answer to:your names." Those present answered t 3 their names, signed the roll as jurors, and selected Mr. Thomas Wright, of Halton, to act as fore- man—a position he has filled for many years. Foreman and jury were sworn to" true presentment make with- out fear, love, favour, or affection," and to " present no man out of malice or hatred." There was, however, no culprit awaiting judgment, and there was no complaint of parochial remissness made. Messrs W Nixon and T S Burgess, were appointed burleyrnen and Messrs J Newport and T Potter were elected constahles. The deputy high steward delivered a charge full of historical reminiscences. Be stated there was an unbroken record of Balton Court beet from 1347. in the reign of King Edward 111., or some- thing like 550 years. There were many peculiar customs of the court which had fallen into disuse. There were the officers kaown as appearers, whose duty it was to moderate the fines and amercements upon those unable to pay the penalty imposed. There also used to be appointed an ale conner, for the purpose of going round to the various public-houses to taste the ale and see if it were of good quality. " Conner " was one who knew what good ale was, and if there was any volunteer, the court might revive the office. There were also many curious charges made which had, however, been corn- muted into some other form. These courts were origin- . atel for the preservation of peace, for the adjustment of oEfences of a mioor character, and for the redress of private injuries.—After the closing of the court, dinner was served under the presidency of Mr Kirkconnell. ; The chief toast was the health of the Queen as " Duke of Lancaster and Lady Paramount of this manor," ' proposed by the Chairman, who also gave" The Prince and Princess of Wales " and 'the Bishops and clergy- ' men and Ministers of all denominations."—The Vice- ; chairman in appropriate terms proposed the health of the deputy-steward, who responded in suitable terms.— The Chairman then gave the toast of" The foreman of tbe Jury." of whom he spoke in high terms of apprecia- tion.—Mr Wright duly acknowledged the toast.

div.head: GOOD SQUARE MEAL.
div.p: A GOOD SQUARE MEAL.
There is nothing better on the face of the earth than a good square meal, if only, as the Yankees say, you can manage to "get away" with it.

A good square meal is a full and hearty meal, and commonly includes numerous articles of food. To eat such a meal, being keen set and free from care, is one of the few perfect pleasures; and to digest it is to have one's strength renewed to fight the world, the flesh, and the devil.

_ Blessed is the man who can eat a good equare meal and carry it off on his stomach as Samson carried the gates of Gaza on his back. That, however, was just what Mr. R. W. New. of 179 High-street, Ryde, 1.W., could not accomplish. He ate the meal—and then came trouble and the self-accusings of a man who has sinned in the face ard eyes of light and knowledge. He knew better—he says so himself—and yet ate the tempting square meal. " FLa• a long time," says Mr. New, in a little letter dated January 6th, 1900, " I suf- fered greatly from chronic indigestion and general dis- order of the stomach."

"Nothing that I ate agreed with me, and if I did venture to take a good square meal it seamed to Jus like a lump on my chest and cause me much difficulty in breathing." Of course it did ; what else ? And therein is one of the chief abominations of dyspepsia. You need food, must have food, Nature so decrees ; still, when you eat you are punished as if youfiad violated all the physiolo- gical commandments in one transgression. It is bard lines, and no mistake. When Mr. New adds that he was in much pain from wind-spasms, and that the secretion from his kidneys was thick and muddy, no dyspeptic will hang fire an instant on believing him ; for the foci system is pra tically the wh,le man, and the stomach poisons g through him as water is soaked up by a lump of sugar. In fact, Mr. New himself puts this point as neatly a possible :—" My entire system was thrown out of gear," he says. He was afraid (and no wonder) that if matters went en so much longer he would have to give up work. 'One day," he tells us, " I was r,lating my case to a gentleman, in hope that be might be able to suggest some remedy I hadn't thought of. And he did. He said If I were in your place I should take Mother Seigel's Syrup and lose no time about It.'

. _ "After the first few does of the Syrup I was immensely relieved, and by keeping on with it I was soon thoroughly cured. Considering how long I bad suffered, and how bad I was, I think that comes pretty c!ose to being a miracle. You may publish my case as you like. I can now eat a square meal and get the good of it."

div.head: ALLEGED DEATH FROM OPIUM AT
div.p: ALLEGED DEATH FROM OPIUM AT
RUNCORN.

On Monday afternoon. Mr. White, deputy coroner, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, on the body of Mary Wood, aged 63 years, of 13, Stonehille, who died on Friday last.—Peter Wood, husband of the deceased, said eight years ago Dr. Mangan recommended his wife to take opium for giddiness in the head and she had since been in the habit of taking small quantities of laudanum. Last week she became very ill and he called in Dr. Robinson, who forbade her to take any more laudanum. The doctor gave her some medicine. She suffered from diarrhcea and vomited a good deal.— Haniaah Bennett, a neighbour, gave similar evidence.— Dr. Robinson said the deceased's nerves were affected. She seemed to be lightheaded.—The Deputy Coroner said the necessity for this inquest arose from the fact that Dr. Robinson did not feel justified in giving a certificate of death in a form which the registrar could accept—Dr. Robinson certified that death was due primarily to the "opium habit" and secondly to sickness, diarrhces and collapse. Of course, if the woman died from taking opium her death was not natural. From the evidence there seemed to be nothing special in the case. The deceased appeared to have taken laudanum a number of years ! under the advice of a doctor, but whether or net Ole I had taken sufficient to do her harm there was nothing to show. She aeemed to have taken the opium in mod- erate quantities, and prohably there was opium in the medicine Dr Robinson prescribed. If there was not he notut have thought she would be b-tter without it. The jhry vtorned a verdict that the deceased died from collapse consequent upon sickness and diarrhcea.—lt was stated by Detective Gregory that the husband was in exceedingly poor circumetances, and the foreman of the jury, Mr Rolonrt Wright, on behalf of the Jury handed him 12s, the fees received by the jurymen.
Spiritualist Funeral at Warrington.

The interment of the remains of Mrs E Stout, wife of the President of the Warrington Spiritualist Society, who died on Thursday of last week after being ill for several months,took place at the Ceme- tery on Saturday afternoon. According to the express wish of the deceased lady, the service was conducted in accordance with the views of the body with which she had been connected. This being the first spiritualist funeral in Warrington, a con- siderable number of persons gathered to witness the ceremony, many probably out of curiosity, but also many in evident sympathy with the bereaved family. As the two chapels vverE. undergoing repairs and alterations, the whole service was conducted at the graveside. Mr Pemberton announced a hymn from the society's hymn book. commencing "Day by day the chain grows longer, one by one now links are joined," which was heartily but reverently sung, after which Mr. E. Marklew offered an invocation, at the close of which he spoke for some time on the cause of the , assembly and bade them instead of mourning rather to rejoice that their sister had entered into the higher life. A hymn commencing "Spirits bright are ever nigh " was then sung, after which Mrs. Porter spoke earnestly upon the lessons to be de- rived from the calling away of their sister. As a concluding hymn, "Nearer, my God, to Thee," was sung, after which Mrs Cropper closed the service with prayer. Instead of the usual practice of throwing handfuls of earth upon the coffin, flowers were strewn. There were several beautiful wreaths from the society and personal friends. Messrs Mounfleld carried out the funeral arrangements in satisfactory manner. ASK for CUNNINEIHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL YATERS.—Advt

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
ENGLISH CUP.
Earlestown v. Swinton Town.

Although Swinton Town came out of the hat first in the draw for the second round of the qualifying stages of the English Cup, for some unaccountable reason they decided to play the match at Earlestown. If the public do not support Swinton as well as,if not better than they do at Earlestown, to say the least of it they are a poor lot. If the visions of a gate of ten or twelve thousand lured them to change the venue of operations, they were never more rudely disappointed than when they turned up at the Mesnes to find five or six hundred spectators waiting to welcome them. One of their Committeemen said during the match that they had been informed that Earlestown regularly drew " gate-. " as large as many a first league club do, and that had they known that they were going to pool a gate of a paltry few hundreds instead of thousands, they would have stayed at home. Perhaps it v. ould have been better had they done so, as the total " gate "receipts would hardly pay their travelling expenses to say nothing of players' wages, printing, &c. However, the spectators, , who did turn up, waited anxiously to see what sort of ' a team Earlestown had to face, very little being known about the Swinton club, beyond the fact that two years ago Wigan County defeated them by a large majority in the English Cup Competition. No opinions were based on that performance though, as a team can change a geed deal in two seasons and again Wigen County were a different team then to what they are now. When the two elevens stepped on the field, they were very evenly matched as regards build, the visitors beiog if anything, rather heavier than the home lot. The players toed the line in the following order soon after 3 o'clock. Earlestown : Chow, goal ; Heyes and Cottam,backs; Pennington, Green and Clibborn, half backs; Bartley, Whitehouse, Linton, Leach,and Settle, forwards. Swinton Town: flammond,goal ; Aidron and Smith, backs ; Aidron, Robinson, and Fletcher, half backs ; Gilbert, Hague, Goodwin, Binks,and Tayler,forwards. The home skipper was successful in the spin of the coin and he gave the visitors the tenefit of the hill, Goodwin setting the ball in motion and Biults and Taylor immediately making tracks for the Earlestown goal. They were however, soon sent to the right about, and a judicious pass from Whitehouse put Bartley in possession, this player careering off along the wing and getting in a fine cen tre which the home forwards utterly failed to utilise. The visiting right wing again ma de a move towards the home goal, a miskick by Cottam leaving Binks sith an open. jog. He got in a lovely oblique shet which Chew dealt with in masterly style, and in a trice the ball was at the other end,where the visitors' goal had a lucky escape. Settle received the ball from Clibborn and passed it to Leach who swung it across the goal to Bartley, this player having the vilest luck in seeing his shot strike one of the home backs and nearly knock him: down, but slowly roll over the line. The ball was kept in midfield for some time after this until from a pretty pass by Whitehouse, Bartley got clean away and easily on k- neeing the backs, defeating Hammond for the first time, with a shot which gave the custodian no chance of sav- ing. This success, which came after play had been in progress half an hour, put new life into the hornesters and there was no holding them in, the interval coming with Swinton in a minority of a single goal. The second half was almost one continual bombardment of the visi- tors goal. The home forwards simply walked round the Swinton half backs, and but for the watchfulness of Hammond, the score against them would have been much larger. The second goal came with in ten minutes of the resumption, Leach heading the ball in and the custodian saying, only to throw to the feet of Bartley, who banged the leather into the net. Straight from the restart, the home forwards were again buzzing round Hammond, and from a pass by Whitehouse, Bartley obtained the third point, Hammond again having no chance of saving. A few minutes afterwards Linton worked himself into a nice position, and then shot the leather hard against the nprieht, Bartley meeting the rebound and putting on No. 4. Before the close Bartley again got the sphere into the net, thus scoring all five goals . a wonderful piece of work for an English Cup tie. In the end Earlestown won by five goals to nil,and they thoroughly deserved their decisive victory too. The visitors were outclassed at every point of the game, and towards the finish the homesters led them a nice dance. After a quarter of an hour's play in the second half, the game resolved itself into nothing more or less than a prolession from the centre of the field to the goal and back again. If the match had been played at Swinton the result might have been different, but on Saturday's form it would not. Far and away the best man on the field was Bart- ley-, the home outside right. Ha played a wonderful game and the way he romped rousse the opposing defence was amusing to watch. He newt' got within twelve yards of the goal with the bail without getting it in the net. The 0pp0..!int,.., custodian got quite used to it and made no attempt to save the sh6ts. It would have been quite useless had he done so. However Bartley's per- formance of scoring all five goals speaks fir itself. Pen- nington and Clibbera were the best of the home half backs and Reyes and Cottarn played very fairly although they had nothing to do in the second half,and the same can be said of Chew. The visitors' custodian was the shining light of his side, his goalkeeping especially when under difficulties being little short of marvellous. Robin- son was the pick of the halves and Binks and Hague were the best of a moderate forward line.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES. Warrington V. Altrinch am. An Easy Win.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES. Warrington V. Altrinch am. An Easy Win.

Warrington had no league fixture on Saturday, but had as visitors the Altrincham team who are members of the second division. The homesters played Dickin- son in place of Fish, who was doing duty for Lanca- shire. and Eden at half back in place of Burgess, other- wise the team was RS usual. Altrincham broueat a representative team. The afternoon turned out fine and dry, with rather a strong cross-brePz and about 2,000 spectators assembled to witness the match. The teams were as follow :

Altrincham : Cooper, full ; H Barnett, Brad- shaw. Tayl.a., and W Barnett, threequarters ; Findlow and Pinder, half backs ; Flampson, Riley, White,Brown, Whitnall, Graham, Norbury, and Charlton, forwards. Taylor set the ball in motion and the home team gra- dually forced their way to the visitors' line. Isherwood made a mark but failed to kick a goal frpen an easy position. done might be v.:lmin the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Act if it was an emergency act done in the interests of the employer. Brookes's action was not an emergency act because there were men to do the work. He (Mr. Scott) did not suggest wilful miscon- duct for a moment, tut the act did not come within the scope of the man's employment. He was emp!ored as a boiler maker, and not to do work of the kind stated.

His Honour summed up at considerable length. He said there was no evidence before him to show that the deceased was aware of the regulations and he (his Honour) found as a fact that he was not• That being so, Mr. Scott still said it was deceased's duty to carry out the rules and when he dis- covered tilt, escapes he ought to have gone to the furnace foreman or the foreman ot the stove cleaners. Altbouch there was an unexpected escape of gas theie was no emergency tor him to remedy. it. He ought to have gone to the persons named. The answer to that was that there was not evidence to show that he knew he ought to hwe gone. The manager of the works said Brookes was a man of ex- perience and be wculd be a proper and right person to remedy the defect so far as knowledge was concerned. He was capable of remedying it and in the emergency he did so. He found OR the facts of the case that the accident did arise in the course of the employment of Brookes, and it was an emergency which he acted upon in the interests of his emptoyers. He awarded the £3OO claimed (the amount not being disputed), with costs on scale C.

div.head: WARRINGTON MAN KILLED AT MIDDLESBOROUGH. The Result of an Escape of Gas.
div.p: A WARRINGTON MAN KILLED AT MIDDLES- BOROUGH. The Result of an Escape of Gas.
£3OO Compensation Awarded,

An important claim under the Workmen's Com- pensation tict of 1897, was heard by his Honour Judge Gwynne James, at the Warrington County Court last Thursday. Georgina Bro.okes,who resides at 67, Howley-lane, claimed the sum of £3OO from the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, cc hick it was alleged was due to her, owing to the death of her husband, whilst follow- ing his employment as a servant of the firnt at Middlesborough. Mr F Green, barrister of Liver- pool, appeared on behalf of the plaintiff and Mr Leslie Scott, of Liverpool, represented the Ocean Accident Insurance Company, on whom the liability fell, in accordance with their agreemen!; with Messrs Pearson and Knowles. Mr. Green,in opening the case, said that Mrs. Brookes wee the widow of a man named 'themes Albert Brookes, who was a foreman boiler maker in the employ of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles. His Honour would not be troubled with any question of figures or amount, the point raised being as to whether the man met his death whilst following hie employment. It appeared that the respondents were under contract in 1899 to erect an iron blast furnace at the works of the North Eastern Steel Company Acklam, Middlesborough, and it was in the course of the carrying out of this work that the accident happened. Brookes was a fore- man, not simply to superintend the operations, but he took an actual part in the work. The work which had to be done was represented by the model produced. The furnace was built, and it was necessary to erect three duet catchers, cylinders through which the fumes of gas from the furnace passed, and the dust was deposited. When the gas had passed through the three cylinders it ought to be comparatively free from dust. Toe accident harpened on the 29th of March of this year, when the work had been almost completed. The furnace had been made, one dust catcher was quite complete, the second was not quite finished, arse the third was in process of con- struction. But there was a valve which was fixed by the respondent's men at the bottom of the connecting branch between the first and second cylinders, the ob- ject being, when this was closed, to keep the gas from the dust. There was a means provided cf allowing gas to get to the main, by what was callel a by-pass. At the time the valve had been put there and was supposed to be keeping the gas from cylinders number two and three, the men still continued to work on the second and third weich were not completed. The Northern Steel Company had, however, commenced to use the furnace ; this valve being put there so that the gas in the ordinary course would pass down by means] of a by-pass and not go in the other cylinders. Number I two cylinder was finished with the exception that the top: plates had not been fastened on, and number three cylinder, in which the men were work- ing at the time of the accident, was not rivetted. The large iron plates had been put in position and the men were riveting them,scaffolding having been fixed both inside and outside the apparatus. On the morning of the date of the accident the men who were working here, felt they were becoming affected to some extent by the gas escaping. In the afternoon they felt it more severely and tound it diffi- cult to continue their work. They complained to Brookes, the foreman, who, of course had charge of the work they were doing. He was at the time working on another part of the apparatus and when he received the complaint he went round to see what could be done. He came to the top of the furnace by means of a boil*, and in order to stop the esc spe, which he assumed WAS caused by the valve not being tight eu,ugh, he went down the connecting breach to attend to the leakage. A bucket, containing loam, was lowered to him by means of a rope and he emptied it and placed the loam round the valve. The I men were proceeding to lower a second bucket. when Brookes was seen to fall. It was assumed that the gas had taken effect on him, and another man went to ren- der assistance bue he was "gassed." Two other men were also overpowered. Unfortunately the deceased was subjected to the escape longer than anyone else, as all the other men were taken out first and recovered. Brookes vemed to be left to the last by come oversight, and consequently he died. Georgia t Brookes, the widow of the deceased gave I evidence.

In cross-examination by Mr. Scott she said that her husband had from time to time been engaged at the Mid- dlesborough works, before the date of the accident, James Ho'croft, an employee of Messrs; Peatson and Knowles, spoke to witnessing the accident. He saw Brookes fall on the valve which was seven feet six inches in diameter and he went down to his assistance but he was overpowered.

By Mr Scott The furnace had been taken over by the Steel Company for some little time and was in blast. He did not know whose duty it was to attend to the valve and ',el that it was properly closed. Witness was of the opinion that it was Brookes's duty to do what be did. He knew the gas was very dangerous. Mr Scott: 1:03 you know there are rules at the com- pany's works, of a very strict kind, as to who shall attend to escapes nf gas? Witness: I have not seen any. Mr. Scott: Have you heard there are such rules? Witness: No sir.

His Honour gaid he understood that Mr Seott's point was that the accident occurred, not within the meaning of ths. Act, as Brookes practically did a thing which he ought not to have done and trespassed. I Mr Scott: Yes, to put it as high as possible. I For the defence, Charles Hornung, the manager of the North Eastern Steel Company'a works, gave evidence. Be stated that the gas which escaped from the furnace was very dangerous and contained carbon and oxide,and in consequence of that there was a special et aff ef men, with a fereman over them, who received reports of leakage and remedied them. There were various methods adopted by the stove cleaners for dealing with leaks under different circumstances. The valve could not be made an absolutely tight fit and if there was oc- casion to Close it absolutely tight, it was necessary to cover it with loam or some such substance. This should be done when the works were standing. On the previous Saturday or Sunday the ;valve was covered with loam, to a depth of nine inches. The loam was put on by one of be I stove cleaners. It was not the duty of anyone but the foreman of the Stove cleaners to see to the stoppage of a leakage. They had printed rules at the works with reference to the reporting of escapes of gas, a copy of which he now produced. He could not say where they were put up, but they were given to the workmen employed by the firm. By Mr Greer : The deceased had been at the works from time to time previously,and bad had to deal with escapee of gas. He had always reported them in the manner described. The work of lemming the valve required experience, but it did not require any more knowledge than the deceased possessed. Nevertheless the deceased would not have been allowed to remedy the escape, even if he had asked permission; William M rks, the furnace foreman, agreed with SI Hornung's evidence as regarded the regulations. He didr not receive any report of a leakage. If any report had been made to him he should have referred the matter to the foreman_ of the stove cleaners.

Frank Bell, the foreman of the stove cleaners, said he did not recite any report of the I:•altage. William Peet, a furnace foreman, said he had a con- versatioo with the deceased the mo:ning previous to the date of the accident. "P:ey were talking about the blowing of ths new fumy... and he (witnss) told Brookes that the gaa was always very bid at fir3t, and he had better not ao into the dust catcher for a few days. D 'ceased said he would not as he had plenty of wok outside.
Hi,; Honour : According to your strAtemeot they our,ht not to have done any work at all at that,
witneEs : I should not hnve done any.

Mr. Scott then addrealeci the court for the &Fence He said that Brookes might have bad sufflaient know- ledge to do the work, but that was immaterial. Ho was not employed for that purpose. The doceased was employed by the respondents as a boiler maker and he had been concerned in tF.re con- struction of this apparatus. The danger which arose from the gas was not connected wi'h the con- struction of the apparatus, but was caused by the Use of it, by the purchasers—the Steel Company. The part in which the leakage took place had passel out of the hands of the contractors into the hinge of the pur- chasers. Legally, and this was important, the workmen of the builders, had no business in that part of the apparatus which had been taken over by the Steel Co. The conversation whi;,•tr took place between Peet and Brookes had perhaps struck his Honour as drawing the inference that it was perfectly open for Brookes to go into this part of the apparatus because he had work to do there. If he bad gone for the purpose of doing work within the, extent of what he had to do in the course of his employment, he had a right there. But he did not co to do any work, and tbe,c- fore the interference which at first eight seemed to be tbe mule to draw from the conversation, beearne entirely erronous. Hs went there to do something which it was the duty of other people to do There was a special an of men employed by the Steel Company for the purpose of dealing with leakages because it was very dangerous. Dcceased%; duty, if he was interfered with in his work by the escape, was to report the matter to the foreman in charge.and it would have been remediPd. There was no sugges-ion that it was necessary for him, in the interests of the respondents to do what he did. A distinction was laid down in some cares where an act was committed which I was beyond scope of the emplumeat. The act j

div.head: ACCIDENT IN A WORKS.
div.p: ACCIDENT IN A WORKS.

A Warrington Boy's Fingers Cut Off. At the Warrington County Court last Thursday, before his Honour Judge Gwynne James, Charles Brown, aged 14 years, reaiding at 2,Portland-street, claimed compensation from Messrs Silcock and Sons,Bing-street,for injuries received whilst fcllow- ing his employment at their works. Mr. Browne appeared on behalf of the plaintiff and Mr.Unsworth represented the defendants. The case for the plaintiff was that he was em- ployed by the defendants as a needle winder, and part of his duties consisted of feeding the boiler. On the day on which the accident happened, May 11th. he was winding with a needle, and when it was full he took it to the foreman to examine it. He had just been to the foreman when he saw a boy named Wilkinson, who was formerly employed at the works as a winder. He allowed Wilkinson to do some winding and went to attend to the boiler. As he was coming away from the boiler he slipped cn the oils floor and his left hand was caught in a cog wheel, which was unfenced and which had since been fenced by order of the factory Inspector. Two of his fingers were cut off. Mr Browne thought the case came under the Employers Liability Act. His Honour: I hope before long we shall see the whole of the provisions of the Liability Act brought within the Compensation Act. It would be far le.,s expensive and more expeditious. Plaintiff gave evidence in support of this state- mext.

For the defence a witness named Ernest Wilfred Sewell, said he asked the boy how the accident happened and he said "I wai sitting on the shaft- ing and got fast.' The shaft revolved very slowly, making it possible for a lad to sit on it without being thrown off. Another witness named Wilkinson, who, it was stated would have been able to hear any convene- tion which took place, said he did not hear Brown make the admission. Mr. Unsworth contended that the accident did not arise out of the employment of the plaintiff, as he was sitting on the shafting and idling his time.

Ili Flonour said it had not been proved to his satisfaction that there was wilful and serious mis- conduct. It was not proved that the boy sat. on the shafting. He made an award for the plaintiff of 33. per week from June 4th, costs to follow on Scale B.

A Word of Encouragement to Liberals of Warrington. Sir,—When I heard the announcement of the poll on 'flaursdav, October 4t4 and .tanding as I did amongst COMO of the most sound Liberals of Warrington I was not surprised to hear how some few of them took their defeat. To such I should like to offer a word of encouragement. Now, taking a general view of the matter it is indeed encouraging to those who will take time to think, that the total number of votes in this election is 9361 on the register. Now in view of this fact try and imagine a Tory not recording his vote after being appealed to by his party, especially when the patriotic feeling of his country is at its climax as a re- su't of the war in South Africa. I take it that the 4468 votes which were given to Mr. Pierpoint is the total (Tory) strength of Warrington, per- haps five or ten per cent. more as there have been within my own experience in this Election good Liberals who say the Tories have got us in a mess so let them get us out. They will do, I have no doubt, but I am sorry they have not a much stronger Opposition so that they could not, as it were, settle this critical business within the timits of their own party. However. lam proud to think that Parliament will be much as it was before the dissolution, and that after the Salisbury and Chamberlain appeal tolthe electorate. They have found ere this that the" man in the street" cannot be hood- winked by their cunning schemes, especially remember- ing that it is costing him dearly already. After being so patriotic in contributing to the various Transvaal Relief funds, it is, I think, freely admitted on both sides that never was there a period in the history of England in which the working classes rose to such loyalty and generosity. So of " Pay, Pay, Pay ' we've had quite enough Remembering what we've got to pay for our own food stuff And before the matter's settled. We shall all be getting nettled With the everlasting sting of the" Pat, Pay, Pay." I am, yours etc, G. H. WALKER.

Municipal Election Compromises. Sir.—Now that the fever caused:by the General Elec- tion bas subsided, perhaps the working men of War- rington, might endeavour to take some interest in the municipal affairs 3f the Borough. With your permission I would like to call their attention to the scandalous compromise effected last year, by the local political organisations, who, by their action have gained for their nominees absolute security, whereby the same enter- prising body, who at present adorn tbe Council, can go back and congratulate each other on their statesman like method of "Bluffing the Electors," out of their right to be represented by whom they choose. To put it briefly, the clubs say, we shall choose a candidate for you, and you must have him, whether you like him or not. If you attempt to put forward one of your own selecting, we will combine our forces against you. Can the aboveo method of dis- franchising the borough, be called English, and can any of your readers say whether such a thing has occurred in any other borough in England within recent years. 1 'can imagine what would be the result of such an attempt in, say Salford or Manchester. There would be an Independent Candidate run in each vacancy as a protest, and how the workingmen of Warrington can swallow this palpable piece of jobbery so cemly, I for one tail to understand. Mr. Crosfield said, that the increased rraj lrity of his I opponent, was due to the apathy of the Radicals in the district, not a bit of it, a great part of that majority. was due to the "Lamb laying down with the Lion." , policy, adopted by the Radical organisation, twelve ' months ago, which produced " nausea." and little I wonder, when we look back on the grand traditions of Liberalism, as pioneered by Glad- stone, Bright, Harcourt and others. If the local Radical organisation cares for and wants to gain confid- ence of the workingrnan,'they will have to demonstrate in a practical manner, that their affeetion goes a long way deeper than his vote. The sooner the workingmen determine to sweep out the councillors who got elected as " Independent," and soon forgot jt, and who are now great guns in the clubs, with a few of the others to keep them from wearying in their retirement, and put in their places workingmen with backbones stiff enough to resist the pressure of the political organisa- tions, the sooner will this borough show some signs of progression. The clubs say that we cannot do it, what is it going to be, the clubs or the people.—Thanking you in anticipation,—l am yours re spe, tfullv, MARTIN FLANAGAN,

div.head: Sir J. T. Brunner M.P,, and Mr. Samson.
div.p: Sir J. T. Brunner M.P,, and Mr. Samson.

Sir,—Since Mr Samson has reproduced in the columns of the Daily News and other papers, one of his election placards, perhaps you will allow me space in which to answer him. He first quotes from my Election address the words, "I have never said or do not say now that the war was unjust,for the reason that it was we who were first attacked." The words I have here put in italics Mr Samson throughout the contest consistently slurred over or overlooked. The Boer ultimatum in my view, put the justice of the war beyond questinn. Anyone who had been present at the Westminster Palace Hotel on Feb 14th and had heard the speeches there de- livered, would have seen that the part of the resolution Ideclaring the war to be a crime and a blunder when Itaken in its context and with the speeches then made, speeches almost entirely occupied wich protests against the bungling of the negotiations, the buying of the South African press,and the intrigues of the Capitalists, was not inconsistent with the view expressed in my el- ection address. Not a word was uttered at the West- minster Palace Hotel in opposition to the idea that we must defend her Majesty's dominions and ourselves when attacked. It is absolutely untrue that during the election I held my tongue and said nothing. All through the contest my supporters and I fought hard against the Government's mistakes, both before and after the war began. And what I said at Davenharn in this re- snect was that I had been unable to talk to them. at Davenham about the origin of ths war. Mr. Samson then attacks ms for having taken Oa chair at the meeting in Liverpool On May 30th last. I Rive you a copy of the resolution drafted by 1119 and put by me to the meeting :—" That earnestly hoping for a speedy close to the deplorable conflict now raging in South Africa—which it believes could have been avoided by a wise and honest statesmanship, the meeting is strongly of opinion that the timely grant of a just measure of autonomy to the inhabitants of the two South African States is ess,ntial to the prevention of a similar strife in the future." Mr. Samson throughout, in this :case also, slurred over the important words. Surely this resolution exactly represents the views of all Liberals with regard to the settlement ; and it appears to me to be precisely what the Government has since proposed. The words of Mr. Stanhope's amendment, for which I voted, exactly express my position now, during the election and before the election. Mr. Samson is surprised at what I said at Davenham on the 16th. His simplicity is almost amusing if he really thinks that the phrase" You may call me a pro- Boer if you like" is an admission that I am a pro-Boer. This rhetorical invitation, you will observe, was offered to a small knot of my supporters in the Liberal Club at Davenham, supporters none of whom, I know perfectly well, would think of accepting it. The term "pro-Boer" has been from the beginning in- tended as an insult, and as such I still regard it. I repeat. for Mr. Samson's edification, lam not an enemy of my country,l am not a Pro-Boar.—Yonrs,&-L, JOHN T. BRUNNER. Druids' Cross. Wavertree, Liverpool. October 24th, 1900.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. Two Field Cornets and 35 Boers Captured. -
French's Fighting March.
The War Office on Thursday issued the fol- lowing from Lord Roberts : PRETORIA, OCT. 24, 10.10 p.m.

French is continuing his march from Bethel and expects to reach lieidelburg on the 26th inst. He reports a little fighting every day, and Second Lieutenant N Calvert and one ser- geant of the Carabineers were killed. A few other slight casualties have taken place. On the 23rd Hickman, commanding a portion of Paget's mounted troops, captured four waggons and fifteen prisoners. The following day Colonel Aytoun," Queens- land Mounted Infantry, with a small farce cap- tured two qeld-cornets—Doonsen and De Beer —and five waggons. One man of Colonel Aytoun's was wounded. On the same day Lieutenant-Colonel Hunt, with three squadrons of Yeomanry cavalry, captured 35 prisoners. A very large number of cattle and 65 prisoners in all have been taken by Paget's force during the last three days. Lieutenant Sewell, Royal Engineers, and ten men of the Rifle Brigade, who were taken prisoners on the 9th just;, reached Greyling- stad on the 23rd.
_ A patrol near Jagersfontein road disturbed a party of Boers attempting to destroy the rail- road. Two of the Boers were killed. Fuses, nipper, and a quantity of dynamite were found.

div.head: Late Lieutenant Hanbury.
div.p: The Late Lieutenant Hanbury.

Lieutenant E. M. Hanbury, killed in action lately in South Africa, is officially described as of the 3rd South Lancashire Regiment (depo', Warrington.) The deceased officer formerly served in that battalion, but has for some time held a commission in the 2nd Line Battalion of the East Yorkshire Regiment. Probably at the date of his death he had been in some way temporarily con- nected with the 3rd South Lancashire, which may explain the discrepancy. The late Lieutenant Hanbury was an officer of much promise, whose loss has been greatly deplored. He was a son of the Right Hon. W. Hanbury, M.P. for Preston.

THURSDAY—Mr. T J Gillespie (in the chair). Colonel Wool. Messrs. W. Collinovood and ti. Stone. FIREwoaKe.—A. youth named Bernard Francis was sum- moned for dischargins fireworks in the street on the 12th inst.—B.S. Bancks said the defendant was diseharging fire- works in Cross-lane. Harlestown. He let one off immediately in front of a lady who wts passing along the footpath.—A fine of Is and costs was imposed, the Chair- man remarking that the defendant had got off vesy easily. If there was any more of this nonsense he would be severely fined. A WRETCHED HOME AT HARLE9TOW2C—JOhn Broster and Hannah Broster. of trlestown, were charge I with having neglected their five children on October 19th and other dates. —Mr. J. W.Knowles prosecuted on behalf of the N.S P.O C., and stated that the defendants ought to have a very com- fortable home and every luxury that a workingman could reasonably be expected to possess. The man was a black- smith and earned 353 per week. and there were two sons earning 15s and 83 respectively, which made a total of 58s per week. The man allowed his wife 26s and she also had the money which the children earned. The Inspector of the Society, with Dr.Gange and a couple of police officers would tell the Bench that there was practically no furniture in the house. The children had no shirts or anything of the kind. and what clothing they had was verminous. The house was never 'dean ed, and there were only two or three cooking utensils. Both the detendants were of drunken habits. The house was not fit to live in and the state of the children was such as to cause them unnecessary pain and suffering—ln- spector Hackett described the result of his visit to t!se house on the 9th inst. The chlldrens clothing was verminous and lice were crawling all over their bodies which were black with vermin. The youngest child was the worst of all its head being sore with lice. The bedrooms, landing and stairs were in a filthy dirty condition.—The woman here stated that her husband was not to blame as be gave her his wages regularly—After consultation Mr. Knowles decided to withdraw the charge against him.—De. Gangs gave evidence and in cross-examivation admitted that the woman came to him with a bad leg about six months ago. The injury, how- ever, was aggravate Iby her drinking habits.—The dts'end- ant admitted having neglected the children but said ice was owing to the injury. She promised to make amends in the future.—The magistrates committed her to gaol for a month with hard labour.—At the close of the case Mrs Knowles made a request to the Bench that the cost of the summonses taken out by the Society should not have to be defrayed by them. The cases were taken up by a phil- anthropic society, formed by philanthropic people and the matter would make no difference to the Magistrates clerk. and very little difference to the County —The Bench agreed to this course. R.S.P.C.A. PEISECUTION.—Thomas Kilshaw was charged with causing two horses to be worked whilst in an unfit state on the 16th inst.. and Michael Burke wets summoned for working them.—P.C. Wooff stated that he saw the defendant driving the horses which were attached to a lurry laden with manure, at Winwick. One of the animals was lame in the off-hind leg 1 and the other was lame in the off fore leg. Both appeared to he in great pain.—Kilshaw was fined 20s ad costs and. Burke was orderedl to pay 5s and cpsts.—rhomas• Sumner and James Sumner appeared before the masistrateecharged with similar offences.—Inspector aobinson proved the case and the first defendant was fined 20s and costs, and the second was mulcted in the costs. Bair, ESTRF,ATED.—WiIIiaII HO3 was summoned for being drunk and disorderly but failed to appear.—David Htlwards and Patrick Rice ware thee summoned to show cause why they should not be called upon to pay the sum of £1 each which they hat forfeited on account of lice's non-appearance. B.S. Brindle stated that Roe was taken into custody but was liberated on Edwards and Rice going bail for him.—The magistrates 'ordered the men to pay £1 each, and issued a warrant for the arrest of Roe.

EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON.

ACCIDENT TO A LAD AT EARLESTOWN. On Saturday afternoon,whilst a lad named Harry Warburton, of Earle-street, Earlestown, 5 years of age, was playing with other lads in the street, he fell awkwardly and broke one of his legs. He was attended by Dr. Patterson who set the injured limb.

div.head: P.S.A.
div.p: P.S.A.

The usual weekly gathering of the Earlestown and District P.S.A. Society, was held in the Co- operative Ball on Sunday afternoon when there was a good attendance. Mr. Eaton presided and the principal speaker was \ r G Dring, who has been away for some weeks through illne=s. Vocal items were given by Miss L Wright, and Mr S Dring pre- sided at the piano.

FEVER OUTBREAK AT NEWTON. A serious outbreak of scarlet f.vor has taken place, at Newton. Already several cases have been removed ta the Infectious Hospital at Warrington, and it is feared that the schools will have to be closed. The cause of the outbreak has not, so far, been traced. VIADUCT INSTITUTE BOWLING CLUB,

The closi of the howling season in connection with this club was celebrated en Saturday evening by a knife and fork tea, held at the Viaduct Hotel, Earlestown, when about 30 members were present. After full justice had been done to the good things provided, the cloth was removed, and the subse- quent proceedings was presided over by Mr H Stan- ton. The loyal toasts were proposed and duly honoured, and the toast" Success to the Viaduct Club," was proposed by Mr Stanton and seconded by Mr J Finch and enthusiastically responded to. The evening was spent in a convivial manner, songs being given by MesQrs Stanton, Allen, Williams, Finch, Tarbuck and Gibbons.
GOOD TE3IPLA.RY.

The Hope of Illarlestown Lodge meeting was held in IV argrave Hall, on Monday evening. Bro G Clarke,E T presiding. Invitations were received and accepted from Bro Plant to entertain at the Mission room Haydock, and from the Hope of Sutton Lodge, Sutton. Bro Llatherharrow and Sister Owen appoi,nted to arrange for Haylock,and Bro Roberts for Sutton. Also notice read of a paper to be read at the Great Heart Lodge No. 2363, St. Helens by Bro Brooks C B T Leigh,entitled "Strong Drink v. Christianity." Greetings were received from Bro Watson. D Sec., St. Luke's Lodge No. 46, Dublin. Song, "The Good-bye at the Door." Sister Morley; encored" When I am far from home ;" Lancashire reading, " Grime's New Business," Bro Clarke. The meeting was closed in the usual manner by Bro Clarke. NEWTON TENNIS, CRICKET, AND BOWLING CLUB: The 'annual dinner under the auspices of this club, to mark the close of the season, took place on Saturday at the Pied Bull Hotel. Newton, where about 70 members sat down to an excellent dinner

provided by Mr A W Bishop, proprietor. The post- prandial proceedings consisted of a toast-list, smok- ing concert, and the distribution of prizes to the successful competitors in the several handicaps. The chair was taken by Mr C H Boitner. He was supported by Mr T Simpson, Mr g Grace (acting secretary), Mr H Hindley, and others. After the usual loyal and patriotic toasts had been honoured, the Chairman proposed "The Newton Cricket, Bowling, and Tennis Club." He said all round they had had a very successf al season. In bowling they had been fortunate enough to run up second for the consolation prize of the Lancashire and Cheshire Counties Bowling Association- The prizes having been distributed to the winners, the Chairman Proposed "The President of the Club" (Mr It Stone), and spoke of the keen interest he took in its welfare. They were indebted to him for many things, particularly for what he had done towards the extension of the grounds and the erect- ion:of a new pavilion. The toast was received with musical honours.—Mr McCormick, who received the President's prize for bowling, urged the members to take a keener interest in the game, and not be dis- couraged by the want of success—Mr H }Lindley Prowised" The Hon. Members," and said there were few clubs which possessed such an excellent list of influential bon. members. Through their kindness and support the club was one of the cheapest and most complete in the county. They could always rely upon the hen members when improvements or new work was taken in hand. Musical honours having been accorded to the hon members. Mr Simpson. in responding, said the hon members always had the welfars of the club at heart.—The toasts of" The Hon Treasurer" and "The Chair-
man "were also cordially received.—The evening was plciasantly spent, songs being given bv Messrs S Henderson, S Appleton, R Smith, Randall, and others.

div.head: BRUTAL HUSBAND.
div.p: A BRUTAL HUSBAND.
An Unhappy Married Life at Earlestown.

At the Newton Patty Sessions on Thursday.before Mr. Gillespie and other magistrates, James Eigley, 84, Athol-street, Earlestowo, was charge i with assaulting his wife. Ann Eigley, on October 1311. Mr. J. W. Knowles, who appeared on behalf of the complainant stated that the parties would have been married for 22 years next Christmas. During the whole of that time, Mrs &lc:ley instructed him, her husband had been in the habit of frequently beating her. He used most disgusting language in the presence of his children and of other children and he was what one might term a beastly man. He abused complainant on the 12th inst, knocking her senseless. She had suffered pain in her side ever sine.. On the Monday previous he thrashed her because he had been locked up and she did not bring him food to the lock-up, He had beaten her regularly cier since their marriage. She had summoned him and withdrawn the summons, she had left him, and I tried everything that mortal woman could try to en- deavour to make him amend his ways. The man was a baker and his wages amounted to 34s a week. They had nine children, five of whom were old enough to support themselves. Complainant askel for a separation order, with a reasonable allowance. Ann Eigley, the complainant, gave evidence and told a pitiful tale to the magiallrees. When her husband got drunk he was like a lunatic. Her ribs had never been right since the night he thrashed her. He always beat her on tie back of the held, anci on one occasion when she was in bed he a.wakelei hr ani thrust a lighted match into her eye. He had frequently told her that she would not die a natural death and had threatened to shoot her. He had run the children out of the house with a knife. He brought drunken men into the house so that the neighbours had begun to call it the "Drunkards' refuge." Evelyn E 17.1ev, daughter of the complainant, corro- borated. In describing the scene on the 13th inst. she said she saw her father pelt her mother out of bed. H 3 tried to smother her, pulled her hair, and banged her head on the bed rail. Witness called in neighbours to assist her mother or defendant would have hit her again. Her mother was badly hurt, and her head Was bleeding.. Defendant main a statement to the effect that he borrowed £lOO from complainant's father, which he had been unable to repay. In consequence of this he had been sub:lnc-ea to great provocation. His wife naweed things repeatedly and he had been nearly " c!arnmel "to death. Elia treatment by her had been scandalous and he had been aggravated to do what he had done to his wife. When he came in on the 13th inst, there was no dinner ready, and his wife was beastly dronk in bed. The mazistratea were of the opinion that defendant had treated his wife brutally and fined him 103 and costs. They alse grant() 1 cnnplainant a separation order with 121 per week. An a lvocate's fee was allowed.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By " OvaUsti

Saturday's match was only a practice canter for the first team against Altrincham, who are one of the best clubs in the second division. What a vast diffrence there ii between the football of the two divisions was very manifest, for the Cheshire Ms were no match for Warrington even with the latter in a playful mood. Had the home team been seriously inclined one trembles to think what would have happened to the visitors. As it was they got off with a licking of 22 points to 6, which was hy no means bad, and they did not disgrace them- selves in play either. They are an energetic lot and stored a couple of tries when Warrington were taking things a bit too easily.

The match was a sort of precursor to the tussle with Runcorn to-Jay, and I hope, a forecast also. It looked just like a meeting between the old rivals, for the Altrincham lads were wearers of the green, like their friends across the Mersey. " Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery," we are told, and perhaps ths " Lin- nets " are all tee happier for having youthful facsimiles in another part of the county.

Thou zh the jersey WAi green. the .nactators were not, and only a few of them resorted to Wilderspool for their Saturday afternoon's enjoyment. "Friendly" football is not a paying or attractive game now-a-days. The spec- tator wants the guarantee of excitement as well as foot- ball before he parts with his "tanner" at the turnstiles, and one cannot blame him. It is an Englishman's, as well as a Scot's privilege to expect and obtain value for his money. Nevertheless the Club benefitted to the extent of about £25 by the visit of such tiny stars in the foot- ball firmament at Altrinchana,so that the spectators can- not be said to have neglected the game entirely. There were about 2,000 present and they seemed to enjoy War- rington's easy task and Eden's ambles very much.

Fish and Burgess were absentees from the home team, the former assisting Lancashire to compile 21 points against Cumberland and the latter having a rest, Dickinson the smart " A" teamer got a trial at centre while Eden, the burly forward assisted (?) "Smack " behind the pack Om or two members of the Com- mittee have long hugged the notion that Eden had the makings of a half-back in him, and I suppose they attained one of their chief desires when he was placed in that responsible position. There is no doubt Eden enjoyed the change, so did Bate, for he was always laughing when he was not handling the ball. There was something to laugh at toy, for Eden scored two tries and did his best to obtain more. Of course Altrincham didn't laugh when the tries were scored, but that could not be expected. Warrington people did, for Eden's tries were specialities, and his exhibition all throuzh was highly comical. Lie is not cut out for half back play, and probably his admirers have realised this by now. Passes of the wildest description, headlong charges at the man with the ball, and other mysterious evolutions were alright against Altrincham, but they would be disaatrous in a League match. S)metimes you could not find Eden at all, he was a sort of " Paradise Lost " all by himself, and Bate had to wait smilingly until he emerged from the melee.

Most of the interest wes centred in the display of young Dickinson, who played centre in the second half and should have done so in the first half. He shaped exceeiingly well in my opinion, has a go3d knowled.ze of the game, fields and passes the bill like an old hand, while his stride promises well for future speed. There is plenty of dash about his work And he should fulfil all expectations in the course of a season or two. Bite made most of the play and his con- tinual resource was a mystery to the visitors. Hocken- hall, Isherwood, and Hallam also gave good exhibions, Lawless toeing only moderate. The forwards had a day out and treated the greenhorns very mercifully. Board- man reminded one of a plunging battleship among a floet of canoes, by the way he ploughed through what oppo- sition there happened to be.

There were no Lancashire Cogapetition matches at all on Saturday. and a glorious afternoon was made poor use of. The two counsv matches, Lancashire v Cumber- land and Cheshire v Yorkshire, took the place and the players of the ordinary games. Fish did himself justice at Workington,lhough he was unable to obtain a try. He however placed three goals and led up to other scores by his cleverness so he could not be called idle at all. Tom Williams was the hero of the day and gave an astonishing exhibition at centre, making repeated open- ings for Sam of the same name from Oldham. Fish came back with enhanced opinions ot the Salford skipper and a great desire to play alongside him. The three- quarter who ctannot score next to Tom Williams must be a duffer.

And what of the other match. Poor Cheshire! Draw the veil in mercy's sake. The Cheshire Cheese was wor- ried in such a barbarous fashion by the "Tykes "that not a single self-respecting maggot will henceforth have anything to do with it. Forty points to nil ! Great Scott ! lam almost sorry I live in Cheshire, but the rates are less and that is a consideration. Yorkshire will be so cocky after this that there will be no holding them until they meet Lancashire at Rochdale on November 3.

The committee have selected the team for to-da,y's great match at Runcorn. and there are a couple of changes from the r 'guitar fifteen. Lawless, whose gool form at the commencement of the season has not peen maintained, is relegated to a back seat, and Dickinson comes into the first team. His promotion is rapid—too rapid I think—for it is taarily advisAble for a young and inexperienced player to be introitalei into first-class football before he has "found his feet." On form the lad deserves his place, but it is jut poss•b'e that it may do him more ha,-an than gooi to have to meet first-alass men so soon. However. time wll show better than any- thing else and I hope Dickinson will do himself justice.

Are we going to best Ruocorn ? That is the question, and it has been the question for the last fourtcea years without having had 4 satisfactory answer from a War- rington point of view. 'Nero have been chances in the past but they have come to nought, and th.re is a fine chance of breaking the spell to-lay. Ruocorn are handi- capped through injuries to Butterworth and Warder,and the absence of these two men should make Warrington's chance an excellent one. I had rather the teams had been representative but football has to be taken as it comes, and it is Warriugton's duty to make the best of Rnncorn's misfortune. They had hard luck at Irwell- lane last season, but bad luck is not perpetutl, and I am looking forward to turning the tables this time. War- rington can do it if they try, and I hope they will try as they never tried before.

div.head: ..•••••••••••....116. g ......... ••••• Bold-street Wesleyan Church.— Children's Day.
div.p: ..•••••••••••....116. g ......... ••••• Bold-street Wesleyan Church.— Children's Day.

On Sunday special services were held in the above church for the benefit of the young members of the church. The R. 7 C H Hockea preached in the morn- ing. In the afternoon a children's service was held in the schools. The scholars were addressed by Mr S B Stringer and the Rev Theodore Bishop. The latter gentleman preached in the evening from the words : "I beseech you therefore brethren, by the mercies of God that, ye present your bodies a living sacrifice., wholly acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service:

Death of Mrs. Speakman. It is with regret we announce the death of Mrs. Speakman, the licensee of the Saracen's Head Hotel, Stockton Heath, which took place shortly before two o'clock on Wednesday morning. The deceased lady, who was 61 years ot age, had been indisposed for several weeks, but about a week since serious symptoms developed, which rendered her case hopeless. She was attended by Drs White and Willett. She had lived in the district about thirty-two years, and had been the licensee of the Saracen's Head for fifteen years. She was held in high esteem especially at Stockton Heath, where her loss will be keenly felt. She was of a charitable disposition and took a great interest in the welfare of the poor class of thd district. The funeral took place yesterday.

Prize Distribution.
On Saturday evening the prizm gained by the students attencliniT above ela.ases at the examinatipne held in eon- nectic,n Nvith the 1899 cession, were distributed in the

Viaduct Institute. by Dr. Patterson. •Mr J W Emmett, J.P., presided, and he was accompanied on the plat- form by Messrs C W Emmett, E T Evans, W Davies, .3 II Stott, D Barcroft, W Bradley, and T Ormand (secre- tary). In the body of the hall there were a large num- ber of students, with their parents and friends. The Chairman said he was told that this was a private distribution of prizes,and no speeches were required. He might say. however,that he had been reading an article relating to the opening of the Manchester and Liverpool line and he would strongly advise those who had not read it, to do so, for it contained a good deal of in- formation about the line they were all so very much in- terested in. If George Stephenson could only come back and see one of Mr. Webb's p owerful engines now, he thought it would astonish him. He then formally in- troduced Dr Patterson, who had kindly come forwar3 to distribete the priz-is. (Applause ) Dr. Patterson thanked the committee for giving him the honour of distributing the prizes that evening. Since that Institute had been in existeled, the number of students had been greatly increased. Fifteen years ago there were only 69 students, whereas this year there were about 450. The classes gave opportunities to students on leaving school, which a generation ago were never thourht or. He would advise all students to at- tend the classes, and gain higher knowledge and info,- mation. Dr. Handyside's medal had not been won this year,but one student had come very near to winning it, having obtained 81 marks, instead of nine. (A.ppla.usa.) He then proceeded with the distribution, the following being the successful students : John Aihtoo, John Bailey: William Bailiff, William Ball. Richard Bancks, Thomas Banks, Eliza Bartley, Eloel Bateman' Walter H Beilby. Frederick Bolton, Lily Bradley, Herbert Bradshaw, Lilly Brownlee, James A Bulloek, Edith Bunting, George Bunting, Elizabeth E Catrwright, Samuel Cawley, Olive Clare, Francis J Coakley, Giles Collinge, Albert G Davies, Joseph Day, Albert E Duncan, Henry C Duncan, Richard A Eaton, John F Eckersley. Harry Edington, Frederick Gannon. Ernes' Jones, J3no Kynaston, John H Latham, William H Lawson, Mabel E Leather, Edith D Lyons, Norman Marsh, Martha Mather, Thomas F Mawdeley, Harold Mayor, John .1. Merrick, George H Morris, Louie M ttram, Lizzie Orden, Percy Orman& William E Payne, James A Pendry, William Pilling, Arthur Porter, Charles F Porter' Hannah J Price. John C Rawlings, William T Reese, E:izabeth Roberts, Jane E Robinson, Richard A Robinson, Harry Rylance, William Savage, Edith M Sirett, Selina Sirrett, Walter Smith, Chris. Spencer, Samuel Stanley, William Stephens, Joseph Stringer. Harry Sweetlove, Louie Swindell, William Taylor, Walter W Thompson, Herbert A Waddington, Mary Webster, Thomas Wheatley, Mary E Whittaker, Harry Whittle, Alcx. Mr J H Stott, in moving a vote of thanks to the prize donors, was quite sure that the students at Earlestown had no reason to complain of lack of generosity on the

part of the &mom He was also glad to see that the students of Earlestown had done their part in winning the prize 3. N) doubt the fact that one prize had not been woo was to be deplored, but a high stsndard had _ _ _ _
to b 3 obtained, and his sympathy went to the sttrlent who so nearly won it—he referred to the gold medal.

The prize list was the most generous one he was acquainted with. He was s'amck also with the small ex- pens2s they had in connection with the working of the classes. He was astouoded whoa he saw the items pu

down for maintenance, &c., for where they were now paying tens of pounds for their classes, if they had a technical school they would have to pay hundreds. The classes were conducted in a singularly efficient manner, and at very little cost indeed. (Applause.) Mr. Bradley seconded and said they were to be con- gratulated upon the magnificent and generous prize fund which they had. The idea ivs the mind of the donors was that the students should bs encouraged and he saw no reason why any of tkem should be backward. (Applause.) The vote was unanimously accorded. On the motion of Mr G Collinge, seconded by Mr R A Robinson, a hearty vote of thanks was given to Dr. Pat- terson. Mr E. T. Evans moved and Mr S Williams seconded a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was passed with acclamation. The Chairman, in acknowledging the compliment, ad- vised the students who had been successful in gaining prizes, to still persevere. He had found, during the last 30 years that when students had got a good prirs, they seemed to go out of the classes altogether, and they heard nothing more about them. He wanted young men to go forward, and do more than merely work with their hands at the. bench. He should want a foreman or two shortly, and he did not know where to look for them, and he wanted the students to educate themselves so as to qualify for such positions. What they had got should be an incentive to them to go forward and do what they could during the present session. (Hear, hear.) Light refreshments were afterwards partakm of by all present.
